title: New Apple Watch features may require new legal precedent for privacy
snippet: Two new Apple Watch features may see the device running up against privacy laws in multiple US states. That’s because the new Live Rewind and Siri Recap features audio-record conversations. The devil is very much in the detail here, since neither feature makes audio recordings accessible to anyone, and it seems likely that the issue will need to be tested in the courts in order to set a new legal precedent … more…
fullText:
Two new Apple Watch features may see the device running up against privacy laws in multiple US states. That’s because the new Live Rewind and Siri Recap features audio-record conversations.

The devil is very much in the detail here, since neither feature makes audio recordings accessible to anyone, and it seems likely that the issue will need to be tested in the courts in order to set a new legal precedent … 

Live Rewind and Siri Recap

Apple announced that the latest Apple Watch models support four new audio intelligence features that use the microphones built into the wearable devices:

Sound Recognition, to recognize sounds like doorbells and fire alarms

Music Recognition, powered by Shazam

Live Rewind, to transcribe what was just said if you missed it

Siri Recap, high-level summaries of conversations

It’s the latter two that create the potential privacy controversy, since they involve recording what both you and those around you are saying.

The law on audio recordings

Whether and when it is legal to audio record conversations depends on the state or country in which you live.

Many US states have what is known as a two-party consent requirement. That is, everyone involved in the conversation needs to know that it is being recorded and to give their consent to this. In these states, it wouldn’t be legal for you to use any device to record a conversation with someone else without their awareness and agreement. (There are some exceptions for law enforcement, but these aren’t relevant here.)

In these states, if the Apple Watch were storing audio recordings and making them available for replay, then the law would be clear: consent is required. The complication here is that Apple very explicitly says that this is not the case.

Apple’s privacy measures

Apple clearly gave a lot of thought to privacy, and we recently discussed what the company has said about each feature.

Neither feature operates in the background by default; each has to be enabled. Live Rewind has to be activated every single time you want to use it, and only operates for 15 seconds. Absolutely nobody gets any access to the audio recordings, which are stored only in a secure exclave chip.

If a conversation is detected, audio flows into a protected buffer inside the Secure Exclave on the S11 chip. It is isolated in hardware so that it is inaccessible to the user, the operating system, apps, and even Apple.

The recordings are only stored temporarily, and deleted as soon as they have been used, either to generate a transcription or to include in a summary. 

The legal uncertainty

Despite these measures, however, Bloomberg reports legal experts highlighting the uncertainties created by the new features.

Bloomberg’s Natalie Lung put the question to attorneys in California, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and Washington on 11 September. Those states generally prohibit intercepting a private or confidential conversation without the consent of everyone involved […] None of the lawyers she spoke to was convinced that Apple’s protections would shield a wearer […]

Speech processed continuously, with no conventional recording at the end of it, may still count as interception under state law.

Phil Lauer, a defense attorney in Pennsylvania, said the technology is “very close to being legal, because it’s not an individual who is actually receiving and using this data.” But, he added, “the argument can be made that it’s unlawful” because the device is picking up audio and interpreting it.

“Whether the courts will see it that way, given all the sort of privacy protection things that Apple has used, that’s an interesting question and it’s going to be coming up,” Lauer said.

9to5Mac’s Take

This is yet another example of the law lagging behind technological capabilities. If an audio recording is used to generate a transcript or a summary without that recording ever being accessible to anybody at all, does it violate laws forbidding recordings? The short answer appears to be: nobody knows.

The Live Rewind feature seems particularly benign. It is literally only able to be used to capture the last 15 seconds of what somebody said, and generates an audible alert when it is used, even if the Watch is in silent mode or connected to headphones.

Ultimately, the issue will likely need to be tested in court. The dilemma for Apple Watch wearers is that it is they, and not Apple, who would be held legally responsible should a court rule that the new features are covered by these laws.

title: New Italian unicorn Exein rides the physical AI wave
snippet: Italian startup Exein has raised a $270 million round of funding led by Headline at a $1.7 billion valuation.
fullText:
Europe has a new unicorn: Italian startup Exein has just raised a $270 million funding round led by Headline at a $1.7 billion valuation on the promise of providing a cybersecurity layer for physical AI — an evolution of its initial focus on IoT.

“The concept of Exein is that every device should be able to defend itself, regardless if they are connected to a secure network or not,” CEO Gianni Cuozzo told TechCrunch. The Rome-based company has been doubling down on this approach; its latest product, Photon, is a runtime security solution to prevent attacks at the kernel level of a device.

This approach requires working in close partnership with manufacturers, and Exein says it has been doing so since its inception in 2018. According to Cuozzo, the choice to work directly with OEMs and silicon vendors was driven by the conviction that connected devices were on the rise. 

This created significant tailwinds for Exein, which claims to have secured more than 2 billion connected devices in sectors where cyberattacks could be paralyzing, including aerospace, industrial automation, automotive manufacturing, energy, healthcare, and semiconductors.

The startup expects its growth to be sustained by the rise of physical AI, which uses the same supply chain. Cuozzo noted that his product can cover AI-powered robots, drones, self-driving cars, sensors, smart appliances, and other connected devices running models on the edge.

Investors seem to agree: Exein says that its latest round was significantly oversubscribed. Its valuation has increased thirty-fold since its Series B some two years ago, and more than doubled since it secured equity and debt in December 2025 following its Series C earlier last year.

Besides valuations, AI has also boosted attackers’ capabilities. According to Cuozzo, this is being facilitated by open source models that can run without guardrails, and make it much easier and cheaper to target physical devices in novel ways.

Exein has already seen an increase in what Cuozzo calls “machine-speed attacks,” and intends to respond with a foundational model for physical AI security. The company is currently training the model on machine data and telemetrics, and plans to have it ready in the first quarter of 2027.

In the meantime, Exein intends to use the fresh funding for M&As to complete its portfolio of products, and hire staff to accelerate its expansion in the U.S. and in the Asia Pacific, which currently drives half of its revenue. 

Cuozzo said being spread across three continents has been Exein’s main challenge so far. The breadth of its presence took some adjusting to, but it has borne fruit, he said, noting that the company is “growing 400% year on year.” 

While such growth numbers are often hard to maintain, Exein could get a hand from the European Union’s Cyber Resilience Act, whose reporting obligations kicked off last week. The Act will come into full force in December 2027, and requires manufacturers to “make sure all digital products are safe from cyber threats.”

Pictured from left to right: Gerardo Gagliardo, CFO & co-founder; Gianni Cuozzo, CEO & founder; and Giovanni Alberto Falcione, CTO & co-founder.

Anna has moderated panels and conducted onstage interviews at industry events of all sizes, including major tech conferences such as TechCrunch Disrupt, 4YFN, South Summit, TNW Conference, VivaTech, and many more.

title: Is Big Tech’s AI slowdown a safety pact or a cartel?
snippet: When OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX head Elon Musk loosely agreed over the weekend to slow down AI development, skeptics spotted an ulterior motive immediately. The AI titans had declared that their aim was to "pace the frontier," signing on at least partially to a proposal for embedding third-party auditors, regulating domestic labs, and reaching a global slowdown agreement. Their critics, however, argued they simply wanted to stop would-be competitors, kneecap the open-source movement, and avoid real legal safeguards - some dubbed it an outright "cartel." The truth … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
When OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX head Elon Musk loosely agreed over the weekend to slow down AI development, skeptics spotted an ulterior motive immediately. The AI titans had declared that their aim was to “pace the frontier,” signing on at least partially to a proposal for embedding third-party auditors, regulating domestic labs, and reaching a global slowdown agreement. Their critics, however, argued they simply wanted to stop would-be competitors, kneecap the open-source movement, and avoid real legal safeguards — some dubbed it an outright “cartel.”

The truth is more complicated, according to sources across the industry. The three-step proposal, laid out in an essay by Amodei, is calling for changes long espoused by AI safety advocates. While it could become a substitute for regulation, under Trump, substantial regulation is unlikely anyway. But experts say that on an issue that’s only likely to grow in importance, AI leaders aren’t the best people to lead the charge.

“The industry as a whole needs new champions,” said Nick Reese, an adjunct professor at New York University and the Department of Homeland Security’s former director of emerging tech policy. “We’ve looked at people like Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, and Elon Musk as these people who are closest to the problem and working on it every day, and they’re the ones who know best. But the truth is there’s never been a realistic vision for what we’re building toward.”

“The industry as a whole needs new champions.”

Concerns about AI advancement have been escalating for months, sparked largely by revelations that swarms of agents were behind rogue hacks going on right under the noses of leading frontier labs Anthropic and OpenAI. Reports from both companies fueled the fire, as did the resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who posted a public letter explaining his choice. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he wrote, adding that neither OpenAI nor Anthropic is “acting responsibly” and rather “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

Dire warnings about AI aren’t anything new inside the industry, but Coxon’s letter seemed to break containment. It’s been viewed more than 170 million times on X alone, while Coxon and his story have made the rounds in newspapers and on TV.

To a significant chunk of AI safety researchers and AI nonprofit workers, however, this is simply drawing more attention to an already widely discussed issue. “A lot of people are thinking of this as Dario’s idea, or it’s coming from the CEOs, but that’s false,” said Daniel Kokotajlo, an ex-OpenAI employee who now leads the AI Futures Project, an AI research nonprofit. “People outside the companies have been calling for this for years … There’s been this growing chorus of voices saying, ‘Please don’t build superintelligence soon. We are not ready. You need to slow down.’”

Kokotajlo said that after years of people “yelling at them to do this” — including more than 1,000 AI lab employees signing a public letter from July, which called for a slowdown in AI development after the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident — the CEOs are “now bowing to that pressure and also claiming credit for it, [although] not rightfully.”

Overall, a handful of sources told The Verge they believe that the verbal agreement made by the AI leaders is a step in the right direction. NYU’s Reese said he “do[es] not think it’s all hot air.” Apollo Research CEO Marius Hobbhahn called it “a good idea,” saying “it’s one of the best things for safety in a long time if it actually happens.” The Midas Project’s Tyler Johnston said it was a “good sign.” Redwood Research CEO Buck Shlegeris said it was “some great news — obviously it’s hard to know whether this is going to convert into anything real, but I’m feeling cautiously optimistic.” All agreed, though, that there was still a lot of work to do to make this verbal commitment a reality, particularly when it comes to making it an ironclad agreement.

“It’s one of the best things for safety in a long time if it actually happens.”

Many still question the motivations of AI’s leaders. The larger tech industry has spent years getting ahead of regulation by lobbying for its own preferred rules or promising self-regulation. Big platforms have proposed policies that could hit smaller competitors harder, using altruistic language to justify self-serving goals. They’ve been accused of safety-washing, or making meaningless changes that give the false impression of actual safeguards. It’s no surprise people are concerned this will happen in the AI industry as well, particularly since AI labs’ voluntary safety frameworks have been criticized for years.

Several sources believe that concerns of safety-washing are valid. “There’s a serious concern that they’re not actually going to slow down,” Kokotajlo says, adding that the fear is that “they’ll just bring in some external auditors, do a bunch of safety paperwork — some of which will be genuinely good — but at the end of the day, it actually won’t slow them down very much at all.”

NYU’s Reese compared this gambit to the social media platforms’ playbook a decade ago, when companies began calling for regulatory action to get ahead of impending, less favorable laws. For the AI industry, Reese said, “the hammer may not come in this administration, but I think if there were a Democratic administration after the next election, there would be a really good possibility.”

That kind of regulation would be vital, said Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project. She said any voluntary framework is essentially regulatory capture and that “we should not be letting the foxes run the henhouse. This is not an opportunity for Congress to once again outsource responsibility to industry.” Daniel Lobo-Lewis, co-founder of the Political Integrity Project, said that voluntary regulation will likely go the way of Meta’s largely toothless Oversight Board.

Most people also, however, believe companies are in no imminent danger of regulation, besides the model pre-release review periods AI labs have agreed to under the Trump administration. President Trump posted on Monday that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” He also called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang while Huang was onstage at a conference — Trump told the crowd on speakerphone that recent concerns about AI were a “hoax” and that “the robots will not be taking over.”

As for concerns that regulation could hold back other companies or open source developers, calls for slowdowns have been almost exclusively aimed at big frontier AI labs defined by exact size metrics, many industry experts told The Verge.

With no government AI regulation incoming, the best option may be to push companies into an immediate, measurable, and enforceable agreement. Kokotajlo’s AI Futures Project, for instance, proposed AI labs giving auditors access to their compute budget — and pledging to decrease their compute budget for research significantly, which would then slow down AI advancement and allow other AI labs to catch up. (Amodei’s essay already called for AI labs to allow external third-party auditors — like METR, Apollo, and Redwood Research — to embed within their organizations to some extent and potentially be able to flag, and blow the whistle on, problematic findings.)

“If I am going to die at the hands of killer AI, I want it to be American, not Chinese.”

Arguably the single biggest challenge to an AI slowdown can be summarized in one word: China.

AI leaders and politicians alike have long positioned China as the reason why US AI progress can’t slow down — because no matter how dangerous the technology may become, they’d rather it be in US hands than Chinese ones, and China won’t pump the brakes. Lobo-Lewis compared China fears to the Cold War missile gap. One X user wrote, “If I am going to die at the hands of killer AI, I want it to be American, not Chinese.”

Redwood Research’s Shlegeris said it wasn’t in the best interest of neither the US nor the Chinese government to pursue AI development in a “reckless” way, adding that “it would not be unprecedented levels of international coordination.”

“[People are] taking for granted that China won’t cooperate,” Johnston said, adding, “This is an issue so serious and so widespread that it seems like it’s in everyone’s interest to coordinate on it, in the same way it was in both the US and Russia’s interest to coordinate on nuclear de-proliferation.”

On Monday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun did push back on the calls for a slowdown, calling it “fearmongering.”

The Midas Project’s Johnston and Redwood Research’s Shlegeris both said that even in the absence of Chinese cooperation, it’s still vital to encourage US coordination. And for the Tech Oversight Project’s Haworth, the slowdown presents an opportunity to “position ourselves as the compass for how AI technology can be developed and used.” She sees arguments to the contrary as part of a familiar playbook. “China gets brought up as a bogeyman every time that an industry wants to escape oversight.”

Kokotajlo simply compared the situation to a cartoon he’d seen, with people in a car driving off a cliff. He recalled the speech bubble saying something like, “Hooray, we’re ahead of China.”

“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”

The issue underlying all the recent panic is a milestone known as recursive self-improvement, and based on the industry’s current trajectory, we’re only hearing the beginning of the alarm bells.

RSI refers to a potential industry milestone at which point AI models can train, advance, and create new versions of themselves — all without human involvement. Anthropic has said this point could come as soon as early 2027, and OpenAI’s chief scientist wrote earlier this month that OpenAI is directing a lot of resources towards reaching this goal. Increasingly, engineers and researchers in the AI industry worry that RSI precedes a whole host of new and more serious AI concerns, including more severe cybersecurity incidents that more deeply impact society at large.

Amodei cited RSI as a major factor in his decision to call for a slowdown: “since roughly this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster.” He wrote in his recent essay that RSI is “starting to happen across the industry, including at Anthropic … Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all.” Amodei proposed implementing “some kind of ‘speed limit’” on the rate of RSI and compared it to caps on missile numbers.

In Jacob Coxon’s resignation post from Anthropic, he warned of “superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources.” Many other researchers at leading AI labs echoed his concerns. It’s “hard to overstate how dangerous” it is to speed towards RSI, wrote Jasmine Wang, an OpenAI researcher. Vishal Maini, an ex-Google DeepMind employee, said RSI is “now so imminent that no other option makes sense.”

Fears about RSI can easily turn apocalyptic. “AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” Samuel Marks, an Anthropic researcher, wrote on X “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.” Another Anthropic researcher and team lead, Evan Hubinger, wrote on X that “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” (He put the chance at greater than 10 percent over the next decade.) Alex Turner, a former Google DeepMind employee, wrote that “many researchers believe they are building something that could kill everyone on the planet. It was literally my day job to think about how to stop that.”

Micah Carroll, an OpenAI researcher, wrote that Coxon’s belief is a “cross-partisan position” with research teams across “all frontier AI companies,” and that they all believe that “business-as-usual AI development poses unacceptable catastrophic risk.”

“But,” Carroll added, “we should also not hyperstition catastrophic risks into existence – they can be greatly reduced via safety requirements with teeth, international coordination, and a consensus to not build [artificial superintelligence] unless there are sufficient safety advances to make us collectively confident to do so.”

That kind of “international coordination” is exactly what AI leaders, and the public at large, are now calling for.

“We have never been in a situation where we actually understood what we were driving towards with regard to AI,” NYU’s Reese said. “We’ve always had this amorphous undefined end state that we don’t really understand but we have to beat China to get to. It’s really hard to race when we don’t even understand the path or even understand what the finish line is — or even if there is one.”

title: Here are the requirements to get Siri AI in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 launched today, and with it Siri AI has debuted as a major upgrade to Apple’s assistant. But there are several requirements Apple has in order to gain access to Siri AI. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 launched today, and with it Siri AI has debuted as a major upgrade to Apple’s assistant. But there are several requirements Apple has in order to gain access to Siri AI.

#1: Supported hardware

Siri AI is supported on all Apple Intelligence-compatible devices.

That means you’ll need an iPhone 15 Pro or newer. Even then though, certain advanced features are only available on iPhone 17 Pro and newer.

All Macs with Apple silicon are supported, and iPads require A17 Pro or newer. Any Apple Watch model that can run watchOS 27 is compatible with Siri AI. And all Vision Pro models are supported.

Siri AI is not (yet) available for Apple TV or HomePod.

#2: Device language set to English

At launch, Siri AI is only available for devices where the language is set to English.

Next month, Apple says Siri AI will also support French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

That expansion will presumably come with iOS 27.1, which is launching no later than October 23.

#3: Age requirements

Apple says that Siri AI is not available for users under 13.

There are no exceptions to this requirement. Even if a child under 13 gets parental permission, they can’t access Siri AI on their device.

On a related note, iOS 27 adds a variety of new and improved child safety features.

#4: Outside the EU and China

Siri AI is available worldwide, except in two key territories: the EU and China.

Here is the company’s explanation for these omissions:

EU: “Apple is working hard to find a path forward that preserves its users’ privacy and security.”

China: ”Siri AI and the other new Apple Intelligence features will not be available in China while Apple works through regulatory requirements.”

title: Fleet Device Management joins Anthropic’s Project Glasswing to research AI-powered endpoint security
snippet: Fleet announced today that it has joined Project Glasswing, Anthropic’s controlled-access program for its Claude Mythos Preview. Fleet will use the access to evaluate how frontier AI can strengthen the security of device management systems, protocols, and the infrastructure around them, with a focus on closing the gap between how quickly threats emerge and how quickly IT teams can respond. more…
fullText:
Fleet announced today that it has joined Project Glasswing, Anthropic’s controlled-access program for its Claude Mythos Preview. Fleet will use the access to evaluate how frontier AI can strengthen the security of device management systems, protocols, and the infrastructure around them, with a focus on closing the gap between how quickly threats emerge and how quickly IT teams can respond.

Fleet’s own Road to AI in IT research found that 79% of orgs take more than a day to deploy critical security patches, even as attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities within just a few hours. That gap is the problem Fleet is aiming to close, and the company says early access to Claude Mythos Preview gives it a chance to test emerging AI capabilities against real-world endpoint management workflows before general release.

“The speed of today’s AI-driven attacks has fundamentally changed what organizations expect from their technology providers,” said Gabe Chan, Staff IT Engineer at Abridge. “Vulnerabilities are manipulated by bad actors almost instantaneously now. As a result, vendors must continuously improve how they identify, evaluate and respond to risk. We’re encouraged to see Fleet investing in research that helps strengthen its own security while contributing practical learnings back to its customers and the industry.”

Fleet says the work will focus on understanding endpoint state, identifying remediation priorities, and increasing the speed and safety of internal security operations. Because Fleet is open source, it says it will share what it learns openly so the broader device management and security community can build on it and everyone can become more secure.

“As a company that specializes in making IT and security teams’ lives easier, celebrating Fleet’s founding anniversary with a renewed commitment to our own product security feels fitting,” said Mike McNeil, CEO and co-founder of Fleet. “We are all about community and transparency. Since Fleet is open source, this Anthropic collaboration will help our customers and the wider security community understand where frontier AI can meaningfully improve the security of endpoint management workflows.”

To learn more about Project Glasswing and its participating companies, visit Anthropic’s website.

title: Early Anthropic hire, former METR COO have found a way to rein in rogue AI agents
snippet: Their startup, Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company (AIUC) has raised $40 million in a Series A round led by Ribbit Capital, with participation from First Harmonic.
fullText:
A day after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit his job over concerns that AI could kill us all by the end of the decade, I met with founders and brothers-in-law Rune Kvist and Rajiv Dattani. They think they have a solution that could save us all, or at least help prevent AI agents from going rogue inside enterprises.

“AI is getting smarter at an increasingly rapid rate. The surprising thing about AI is that it becomes harder to adopt and harder to control as AI gets smarter, not easier,” said Kvist, an early Anthropic employee who is also married to Dattani’s sister). Dattani is the former COO of the AI safety research organization METR.

The pair launched a startup called Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company (AIUC) that hopes to bring AI safety to enterprises and companies building AI models and agents. The startup names Cursor, Lovable, Harvey, and ElevenLabs as customers.

On Tuesday, AIUC announced a $40 million Series A led by Ribbit Capital, with participation from First Harmonic. It previously closed a $15 million seed round from Nat Friedman through his fund NFDG along with Emergence, Terrain, and Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann, among others, bringing its total funding to $55 million.

What caught the attention of this A-list group of investors is AIUC’s attempt to apply a familiar cybersecurity model to a new set of AI risks. The company has built a third-party audit and certification layer for AI agents.

“Banks, hospitals, governments and militaries no longer decline to deploy AI because a model isn’t smart enough,” Kvist said. “They decline because they’ve made commitments to their own customers about what a system will and won’t do, and nobody can currently guarantee that.”

Using the widely adopted cybersecurity standard SOC 2 as its muse, AIUC has developed a standard called AIUC-1 and a testing service to validate agents against the standard.

To build the standard, AIUC assembled a consortium of about 250 security and risk leaders — the buyers of agents. “These are the people who we meet with on a monthly basis, and the question we ask them is: When you’re buying agents from someone, what would you look for? What are the questions you’d want to ask, and what would you want to see addressed?” Dattani told TechCrunch.

That feedback shapes the tests. The startup then runs an agent through a suite of some 5,000 tests to see how it behaves in scenarios involving jailbreaks, hallucinations, and data leaks. The results produce a roughly 100-page report detailing where an agent performs safely and reliably — and where it doesn’t. Interestingly, AIUC uses AI agents to run the tests and AI to analyze the data. Humans, however, verify the final audit, Kvist said.

If this sounds a bit familiar, it is. Dattani’s former employer METR, where he was COO from 2024 to 2025 and remains a board member, does similar testing for the frontier labs, though its work until recently has focused mostly on performance (whether agents can reliably complete tasks). METR was one of the independent research orgs OpenAI used to investigate its Hugging Face incident.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has also recently called for the AI industry to pace frontier development, citing a rapid increase in bad-behavior incidents. In his post, Amodei floated the idea of requiring frontier labs to use embedded third-party evaluators to observe and verify safety, and named METR as one possibility.

While AIUC isn’t proposing to embed itself at customer sites, the overall idea is similar: give enterprises an independent assessment of how safe their AI agents are. “Here’s where it passes and where you can trust it. And here’s where there’s concerns. You should be aware of those references before you make the decision to buy,” Dattani said.

title: Salesforce and Nvidia’s new reasoning model is everything the AI labs should fear
snippet: Salesforce Koa is built on Nvidia's open-weight Nemotron model and is trained to do sales, marketing, and customer-support tasks.
fullText:
A new AI model called Koa is one of the biggest announcements from Salesforce this week at its giant Dreamforce tech conference. Koa is the company’s first reasoning model, built on Nvidia’s open-weight Nemotron model. The two companies worked together to post-train Koa to excel at sales, marketing, and customer-support-related tasks.

Koa is a shining example of how the enterprise world’s needs for AI are diverging from what the frontier labs are offering. Proprietary AI labs would rather have enterprises uploading files, code, prompts, and feedback directly into their models and agents, and spending millions to do so.

But with the model, Salesforce is offering its enterprise customers:

an open-weight alternative to closed frontier models

a model trained to do specific work tasks (rather than to solve impossible math problems)

one that has not ingested any actual customer data and therefore cannot leak it to others

a model that helps reduce AI spending, since it uses fewer tokens to do the same work

one that can be automatically routed through an AI “gateway,” depending on the need

and a model that follows all of a customer’s data requirements and security embedded within Salesforce

Koa will be provided as an alternative to the other models Salesforce offers in its Agentforce platform, where its customers build agents to handle rote tasks like answering customer service questions or scheduling appointments.

“We’ve built many small task-specific language models, which are part of Agentforce’s portfolio,” Jayesh Govindarajan, EVP of Salesforce AI, told TechCrunch. “But reasoning has always been something that we’ve relied on the frontier model providers for. Until now.”

Before Koa, if an agent needed to reason through a long-running or multi-step task, those prompts would be routed to a frontier model like Claude or ChatGPT through Agentforce’s AI gateway (the system that decides which model handles which request).

“One of the reasons we hadn’t done this before, train our own enterprise-grade frontier model — we always wanted to — but the challenge has always been the lack of a pre-trained base model to start with. Until Nemotron came along, there was no sovereign American pre-trained model that was available, one, and two, that was state of the art, and, three, that had clear data provenance. We have no idea what Qwen trains on,” Govindarajan said, referring to the popular Chinese open-weight model produced by Alibaba.

Post-training a model like this means taking it from a general-purpose system to one well-versed in sales and customer support knowledge, and to do that, Salesforce and Nvidia did not use any actual data from Salesforce’s customers. Instead, they crafted synthetic data that mimicked customers’ patterns.

“We actually simulated a customer service environment with a persona customer service professional, including irate customers that call into the customer service center, all the way to a sales professional who’s trying to close a deal,” Govindarajan described. 

Koa is meant to be better at the work tasks Salesforce customers want an agent to do — and cheaper, in terms of tokens burned — than sending those same tasks to Claude or ChatGPT.

With Nemotron, “we have a unique architecture for inference to be token efficient,” Kari Ann Briski, Nvidia’s VP of Generative AI Software for Enterprise, told TechCrunch. “It’s kind of the trifecta of things that you need to have: sovereign AI, time to first token, efficient reasoning, for the tokenomics of it all.”

However, Salesforce isn’t exactly abandoning Anthropic or OpenAI. It just announced a partnership with Anthropic called Claudeforce that allows companies to use Claude as their AI interface, while their data remains in Salesforce’s system of records, secured by its infrastructure.

title: Two Galaxy S27 models will get Samsung’s Privacy Display, not just the Ultra
snippet: New reports coming from industry sources close to Samsung suggest the smartphone maker will equip not just the Galaxy S27 Ultra with its Privacy Display panels, but the Galaxy S27 Pro, as well. more…
fullText:
New reports coming from industry sources close to Samsung suggest the smartphone maker will equip not just the Galaxy S27 Ultra with its Privacy Display panels, but the Galaxy S27 Pro, as well.

According to recent reports from ET News, industry sources claim Samsung plans to include a Privacy Display panel on the Galaxy S27 Pro and the Galaxy S27 Ultra. The panel is known internally as Samsung’s Flex Magic Panel, and the new leaked information ties it to the top two flagships Samsung wants to release in 2027.

The Privacy Display was earlier in the year on the Galaxy S26 Ultra. In lieu of offering an anti-glare Gorilla Glass panel like the year before, Samsung opted for a specialized OLED panel that obscured either isolated portions or the entire screen from certain angles. It’s a native form of privacy screen protectors, built into the phone, and with more granular controls over sensitive notifications and more.

On the Galaxy S26 Ultra, One UI allows users to hide notifications from prying eyes, as well as the entire screen or other parts that might contain sensitive information. It’s suggested that the Galaxy S27 Pro’s display will allow users to do the same. The COE elements in the display can be thought of as a sort of polarization, where parts of the screen are blocked from anything other than a head-on view.

	

Previous leaks suggest Samsung plans on padding out its smartphone range with four entries:

Galaxy S27

Galaxy S27+

Galaxy S27 Pro

Galaxy S27 Ultra

With that, the Galaxy S27 line will be overhauled with a new display and overall design that many like to compare to the recently adopted design language of recent iPhone versions. The Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra variants will have a much more robust camera bar/island, with the Pro being a much more obvious little brother to the Ultra than the S+ ever was. At least, in looks.

Further, it looks like the Galaxy S27 Pro will take on the Ultra’s price point, and the new premium flagship Galaxy S27 Ultra will get its own price hike.

Samsung is expected to announce the four new Galaxy S27 devices early next year.

title: MediaTek’s Dimensity 9600 Pro Focuses on Gaming, AI Performance for High-End Phones
snippet: The high-end processor is the company’s first to use TSMC’s 2-nanometer process.
fullText:
MediaTek on Tuesday unveiled its new Dimensity 9600 Pro and 9600M phone processors, both of which highlight support for advanced gaming as well as artificial intelligence features for upcoming phones.

Phone processors are an important component in any device — they help power everything from how fast a phone runs, image processing, games with intensive graphics and running certain AI features on your device without needing to connect to the internet.

The Dimensity 9600 Pro will be the company’s first to use the 2-nanometer process in partnership with chipmaker TSMC, which we’re also seeing in rival chips from companies like Apple’s A20 Pro processor that’s shipping with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. This should mean the processor is denser, allowing for more performance and power efficiency. 

Oppo’s Find X9 Pro runs on MediaTek’s 9500 processor.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

MediaTek says the 9600 Pro will support faster performance and on-device AI features over last year’s Dimensity 9500, and for gaming, it will be capable of console-quality gaming at an exceedingly smooth 185 frames per second.

The 9600M will be the step-down processor meant for a wider range of devices, and MediaTek says that it will still power AI features as well as gaming at the same 185fps.

MediaTek’s new high-end processors will face their most competition from Qualcomm’s Snapdragon line, the latter of which typically powers Samsung’s Galaxy S and Z phones in the US. We’ll soon know what Qualcomm’s next high-end processor will look like, as the company will likely use its Snapdragon Summit to debut it on Sept. 22. But MediaTek’s high-end processors are found in a lot of devices internationally, with last year’s 9500 powering phones like the Oppo Find X9 Pro.

Phones running on MediaTek’s Dimensity 9600 Pro and 9600M are expected to debut later this year.

title: AI infrastructure company Cornelis raises $205M to chip away at Nvidia’s dominance
snippet: The company also announced a product called Active Compute Fabric, a network technology that targets the fact that much GPU time is wasted waiting for data to arrive.
fullText:
Cornelis, a company creating networking technology to help AI chips communicate more effectively, announced Monday that it has raised $205 million in a funding round led by IAG Capital Partners. 

It also announced a product called Active Compute Fabric, a network technology that targets the fact that much GPU time is wasted waiting for data to arrive. Cornelis hopes to address this with a networking fabric that lets chips process and send information at the same time.

The company, which spun off from Intel in 2020, is competing with Nvidia by offering an open architecture, meaning customers can use a variety of GPU and accelerator hardware with Cornelis’ networking fabric. Though Nvidia chips can technically run on other networking fabrics, they’re optimized to run on Nvidia’s own software, making it much easier — and more enticing — for customers to use Nvidia’s full GPU stack. Cornelis is part of a new wave of AI infrastructure companies emerging to break apart Nvidia’s market dominance, piece by piece (or chip by chip, one could say). 

Cornelis has already started shipping its product and is working on a new generation of it, expected to be released later this year.

title: Siri AI Will Have Deep Integration With ChatGPT and Claude Models, Leaked Build Shows
snippet: Siri AI will cooperate with ChatGPT or Claude on certain tasks. The third-party models can even replace Siri altogether.
fullText:
Apple is putting a lot of effort into making Siri AI the next big thing in its product ecosystem, and its recent Surprise and Shine event made it clear that the revamped voice assistant will be positioned as one of the key selling points of the new iPhone 18 Pro.

But apparently the tech giant isn’t wresting its hardware out of competitors’ hands, according to an X post from pdfu, who routinely leaks upcoming iOS and MacOS code. Instead, according to the post, Apple’s AI will feature deep integration with third-party models, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude, with an option to entirely replace Siri with certain GPT models as the on-device agent of choice.

Representatives for Apple, OpenAI and Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The latest private frameworks leaked for iOS 27 and MacOS Golden Gate supposedly include Claude models as part of the model delegation feature, where Siri AI users can ask Apple’s model to delegate tasks to another agent.

In a video pdfu posted on X, Siri passes along a request to Claude to create a reminder in the Reminders app. Claude essentially functions as the on-device AI in this video, with Siri working as an intermediary. And if a given request requires access to proprietary Apple system information, it is handled by Siri AI instead.

Also on display was an even more robust app extension that completely replaces Apple’s own Siri AI model with a different LLM. Using this model manager service on the private framework, pdfu successfully ran GPT-5.6 with Siri’s logged information to execute requests using Siri UI and voice.

The video shows the GPT-5.6 model searching through emails on the device, locating specific pieces of information in the inbox and using that text to send messages to people in the iMessages app. All of that information – usually filtered through Siri AI – can be logged in OpenAI’s web interface for later access on another platform.

Is Apple breaking down this walled garden of its own volition? Probably not. The European Union’s Digital Markets Act, which requires Apple to give third-party developers equal access to its hardware and software features, has largely shaped how the company rolls out its new operating system updates.

The legislation specifically targeted Siri AI and Google’s Gemini AI, ruling that the phone-makers will need to allow third-party AI developers access to on-device software updates in the future to prevent market gatekeeping.

Although Apple isn’t opening its doors to third-party AI companies out of the goodness of its own heart, this is big news for OpenAI and Anthropic, the developers of ChatGPT and Claude.

The two companies are racing to develop more advanced models — and prove their worth to the public — amid a largely unregulated environment.

With the promise of absurdly lucrative IPOs for both companies looming in the near future, it’s likely that OpenAI and Anthropic will continue to try to tap into an outsized market of American iPhone users.

title: iOS 27 adds new opt-in setting for sharing data to improve Apple’s Foundation Models
snippet: After several months of beta testing, Apple released Siri AI to the public today as part of iOS 27 and its other OS updates. During setup, users will see a new prompt asking whether they’d like to opt in to improve Siri and Apple Intelligence. Here’s what that means. more…
fullText:
After several months of beta testing, Apple released Siri AI to the public today as part of iOS 27 and its other OS updates. 

During setup, users will see a new prompt asking whether they’d like to opt in to improve Siri and Apple Intelligence. Here’s what that means. 

Before today, users were asked during setup whether they wanted to help improve Siri and Dictation. If they opted into that, audio and transcripts from Siri and Dictation would be shared with Apple. 

Starting today, when a user enables Siri AI, they will see a setup screen asking whether they want to opt in to “improve Siri and Apple Intelligence,” with two options: “Share Audio and Text” or “Not Now.”

Apple says:

Improve Siri & Apple Intelligence

Help improve foundation models and Siri by allowing Apple to collect and use your text and audio interactions with Siri, Dictation, and Translate.

What’s important to note here is that nothing is changing about the type of data Apple collects if you opt in to this setting. What’s changing is that Apple will now use the data to train and refine its Foundation Models, as well as Siri and Dictation like before.

Even people who previously opted in under the old setting will be asked again when they enable Siri AI. This gives them an opportunity to reevaluate their preference now that the data will also be used to train Apple Foundation Models.

When asking users if they’d like to opt in, Apple makes its privacy protections clear. The company says that Siri audio data, transcripts, and related data are tied to a “random, device-generated identifier that rotates multiple times per hour.” It is not tied to your Apple Account or email address. Apple does not use the data to build a marketing profile or sell it to anyone.

You can change your preference by going to Settings > Privacy & Security > Analytics & Improvements > Improve Siri & Apple Intelligence, and toggling it on or off.

Apple has also published a new support document detailing these settings across all of its platforms.

fullText:
It’s been more than a year since we asked whether Apple should give us the option of choosing our own AI chatbot to replace Siri AI. At that time, the majority of you were in favor.

A developer who has been studying the code in iOS 27 and macOS 27 has discovered that it does indeed appear at least some people will have this option …

In our previous poll, two thirds of you said yes, absolutely, we should have that choice – with a further 15% also preferring it. Only 6% of you were strongly opposed.

At the time, I fully expected Apple to be reluctant to do this, raising its usual objection that opening up the system to third-party apps creates privacy and security risks. Developer PDFU has, however, seemingly found evidence in iOS 27 and macOS 27 that Apple will be supporting this.

The video demo shows them selecting Claude as the AI assistant.

iOS 27 and macOS Golden Gate have private hooks that let apps add Siri Extensions and replace Siri AI’s server backend with third-party models.

First, here’s Claude running as a Siri Extension using the Model Delegation API in App Intents. Claude can appear in Siri’s “Ask…”… pic.twitter.com/OXKHQ4hDY8

— pdfu (@itspdfu) September 13, 2026

You cannot yet activate this – it’s visible in the code but not currently enabled.

9to5Mac’s Take

If this choice is made available globally, I would see that as a win for everyone – even Apple. It’s an obvious win for users, as we can each choose our preferred AI platform and because the competition will drive Apple’s own pace of improvements to Siri AI. 

	

That impetus, along with keeping as many Apple users as possible happy, also makes it a win for the iPhone maker.

However, there is a strong possibility that this feature will only be enabled within the EU, where Apple has already had to make a number of similar accommodations. Whether users in the US and elsewhere will be able to do it remains to be seen.

title: Arm’s new CPU cores and GPUs for Android chips promise ‘desktop-class’ games, more AI power
snippet: Arm has announced its new C2 CPUs for future Android chips as well as upgrades to its Mali GPUs that will take everything up a notch. more…
fullText:
Arm has announced its new C2 CPUs for future Android chips as well as upgrades to its Mali GPUs that will take everything up a notch.

Arm CPU designs are the backbone of many Android smartphone chips, including the likes of MediaTek flagships and Google’s Tensor as well. This week, Arm has announced its C2-Ultra and C2-Pro CPU cores, delivering a 15% boost to single-thread performance and 12% faster app launches, as well as local AI that’s built into the CPU itself instead of offloading to a dedicated NPU or TPU.

Arm claims:

Up to 1.7x performance improvement across the latest AI models

Up to 15 percent higher single-thread performance

15 percent faster web browsing

12 percent faster application launch

12 percent higher multi-thread performance at the cluster level, supporting parallel activity across retrieval, model preparation and application execution

But the more exciting announcement here is the GPU, with Arm’s new Mali G2-Ultra NX claiming to deliver “desktop-class” performance with the help of “AI-native graphics.” Arm says that this new GPU “integrates neural acceleration directly into the graphics pipeline, helping developers deliver richer, more responsive visual experiences within the mobile power envelope and bring neural graphics into production faster.”

	

The new GPU as a whole sees a 14% boost in performance, but also integrates Unreal Engine 5 “MegaLights” while also being able to generate intermediate frames for smooth gameplay or upscale low-res games. 

This could all show up in other form factors eventually, but it’s starting out in phones. Specifically, Xiaomi’s 18 Fold and its XRing O3 chip will be the first to integrate this new hardware, though games that take full advantage of it could be a ways out.

title: macOS 27: new Siri takes on AI productivity apps
snippet: The two most noticeable things about macOS 27 Golden Gate are the newly updated Siri AI and the design changes that make windows and icons more consistent.
fullText:
The two most noticeable things about macOS 27 Golden Gate are the newly updated Siri AI and the design changes that make windows and icons more consistent. Siri AI offers the same features and capabilities as on iOS 27, but the Mac gives it access to different context — and new ways to be useful.

Over the last few years, apps and browsers have tried to learn more about your work and what you want to use AI assistants for, so they can better answer your questions or perform tasks. Today, many top web browsers, excluding Safari, come with a sidebar-based AI assistant that can look at one or multiple open tabs to provide contextual answers. Apps like Highlight, Caddy, and Littlebird can also look at your current window, then use that information as context for your queries.

The new Siri is similar. You can invoke Siri anywhere on your screen, allowing it to answer questions about what it sees, summarize information, or provide you with more details. For instance, if you are looking at an item you want to purchase, you could ask Siri to show you alternative options too. 

Instead of having Siri look at the whole page, you can also select a part of the page via Apple’s new Visual Intelligence features. If you press Command + Shift + Space, you can add the currently focused window to your context for the AI. 

To select a specific part, press Command + Shift + 6 to bring up a crosshair selection tool. After this, you can directly ask a question or perform an image search. Based on your selection, you will also get shortcuts like “Select,” “Add to Contact,” and “Look up Location.”

Image Credits:Ivan Mehta

Apple has also improved Spotlight Search on Mac. You can directly ask Siri questions within Spotlight to get answers from the web, and now you can also select Applications, Files, Actions, and Clipboard to search within that particular area of context. Plus, Spotlight now allows you to run Shortcuts or look up your recent search history.

Since Siri has access to your files, emails, and messages, you can search for a variety of things that you couldn’t before. In tests, I pulled up membership IDs without opening my files, asked for details about an upcoming trip, and looked up the embargo date for an upcoming news story in the works. While I don’t find Spotlight as advanced as the highly extensible Mac productivity tool Raycast, it’s still much better than before.

Image Credits:Ivan Mehta

Siri can also now help you with reviewing documents or performing writing tasks. Since the desktop is one of the better surfaces for writing long text, I found it to be more useful here than on the iPhone. You can do things like select a block of text and ask Siri to proofread it, improve it, or rewrite it. You can also ask Siri to draft something for you within any text box.

Safari, meanwhile, has added AI-powered page tracking, which is useful for keeping an eye on things like price drops, privacy policy changes, or new blog posts on pages when there is no RSS support. Plus, Safari can automatically organize tabs based on topics, which is handy.

Image Credits:Ivan Mehta

One small but neat new feature is that when you download a file or rename it, the system suggests a name based on context in the Finder or when you’re saving the document.

fullText:
DIY home security company SimpliSafe is bringing its AI-powered proactive security feature to the front door. The new SimpliSafe Video Doorbell Series 2 launches today for $199.99 and works with the company’s Active Guard Outdoor Protection (starting at $49.99 a month). This combines AI analysis with live agents to detect potential threats and respond proactively.

When the camera detects suspicious activity — using a combination of on-device AI, cloud-based computer vision, and facial recognition — a SimpliSafe monitoring agent can drop in on the camera to “see, speak to, and attempt to deter potential intruders and package thieves,” according to the company.

The SimpliSafe Video Doorbell Series 2 is a wired doorbell with 2K resolution, a 10x zoom, a 150-degree head-to-toe view, two-way audio, and a built-in siren. It has smart alerts for people and packages, up to five seconds of pre-roll video, and supports dual-band Wi-Fi. The doorbell requires a SimpliSafe base station and keypad and works with any monitored SimpliSafe plan. It can also be used with a self-monitored plan with video recording.

Active Guard was launched in 2023 on SimpliSafe’s indoor camera, arrived on outdoor cameras in 2024, and is now available on the company’s newest doorbell camera. The feature is opt-in, and the agent can only view live footage when the system is armed and has been triggered. Active Guard requires a Pro or Plus SimpliSafe monitoring plan starting at $49.99 a month. In addition to potentially deterring intruders, SimpliSafe says the system can provide emergency services with more accurate information.

The company has published a privacy page detailing how the system works, including that the footage is encrypted (at rest and in transit, not end-to-end) and that it “won’t share camera footage with law enforcement unless required by law.”

Color-coded LED status lights on the doorbell indicate when a monitoring agent (amber) or homeowner (blue) is speaking, and you can create a library of familiar faces so the monitoring agent doesn’t scare the bejeezus out of your dog walker.

Ring offers a similar proactive security feature called Virtual Guard that works with its Ring Alarm system for $99 a month. Having a human be able to see and verify whether there’s any actual danger at your home and potentially act on it has value, especially if you live in an area where false alarms incur fines, but for most people this feels like overkill.

title: Microsoft’s new AI ‘code of conduct’ tells models not to hack systems or trick humans
snippet: The code of conduct lays out general principles that Microsoft AI models should uphold — supporting humans rather than replacing them, for instance, and accelerating human flourishing — as well as specific safety constraints meant to implement those principles.
fullText:
As the AI world shifts its focus to safety and alignment, Microsoft has released a new AI code of conduct meant to guide AI models away from dangerous behavior.

The document is more low level than Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s recent call for pacing the frontier, instead focusing on the values and red lines that guide model training within Microsoft AI. Still, the result is a comprehensive guide as to how Microsoft approaches AI safety and how those ideas are implemented in practice.

The document begins with the prediction that, in the next decade, superintelligent AI systems will surpass human performance in most tasks. “Containing, controlling, and aligning such a powerful force is one of the greatest challenges humanity has ever faced,” the code of conduct states. “We must therefore be completely clear about why we are inventing these systems and how we intend to control them.”

The code of conduct also lays out general principles that Microsoft AI models should uphold — supporting humans rather than replacing them, for instance, and accelerating human flourishing — as well as specific safety constraints meant to implement those principles. 

Under Microsoft’s system, each model has an overarching code of conduct that overrides the preferences of individual users or any specific tasks. That includes “absolute constraints” forbidding cyberattacks, nuclear weapons, or deepfake production. It also includes broader provisions against a general loss of human control.

“MAI Models will not use adaptive, deceptive, self-reinforcing, collusion, or other mechanisms to evade or defeat human oversight so that they can no longer be reliably directed, modified, or shut down by authorized people or systems,” the document reads.

The release comes amid an unprecedented focus on AI safety, driven by a string of rogue-agent incidents, as well as the abrupt resignation of an Anthropic employee, who cited the growing risk that AI would cause human extinction.

Together with Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI, Microsoft has broadly embraced a general approach of pacing the frontier, with particular support for embedded evaluators in AI labs.

“We welcome the research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal,” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella wrote online. “We also welcome ideas like ’embedded evaluators’ and the broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this more than just talk.”

title: SmartGym 8 brings natural-language workout creation, Siri AI integration, more
snippet: SmartGym is out with a massive update today that introduces AI-powered workout creation, management, deeper Siri integration, and several features that leverage the new possibilities of iOS 27, iPadOS, and watchOS 27. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
SmartGym is out with a massive update today that introduces AI-powered workout creation, management, deeper Siri integration, and several features that leverage the new possibilities of iOS 27, iPadOS, and watchOS 27. Here are the details.

I’ve written before about how much I like using SmartGym to track my exercise routine.

SmartGym is an Apple Design Award winner, and it doesn’t take long to see why. Developer Matt Abras is constantly changing, updating, and tweaking the app to make it easier and more streamlined to manage, track, and log gym sessions, improving on what has long been one of the most mature and useful gym-tracking apps on the App Store.

Today, SmartGym is getting one of its biggest updates ever. SmartGym 8 introduces SmartGym Intelligence, which is, in essence, the app’s own take on Private Cloud Compute.

SmartGym introduces its own Private Cloud Compute alternative

As Abras explains, SmartGym is currently not eligible to use Apple’s Private Cloud Compute through the new Foundation Models framework. So, he decided to build his own.

SmartGym Intelligence is private by design. Every request sent to a model is anonymous and disconnected from the user’s identity. Prompts and responses are never logged, cached, or retained by SmartGym.

SmartGym 8 relies on Apple’s new Language Model APIs to extend the Foundation Models framework to frontier models running on SmartGym’s own private cloud infrastructure, while keeping requests anonymous and disconnected from the user’s identity.

SmartGym never connects directly to an AI lab. The labs behind these frontier models never receive users’ prompts, and nothing users submit is used to train their models.

With today’s update, users can now create workout routines with natural language. This means they can type something like “create a push-pull-legs workout with 10 exercises per day. Avoid bench press. Include 2 warm-up exercises per day,” and the app’s new framework will handle the rest.

Once the workout is created, users can send new prompts such as “move leg day to Friday,” “remove the barbell squat,” or “make Wednesday a rest day,” to tweak it even further.

To try the new SmartGym Intelligence, users can go to the Routines tab in SmartGym 8 on iPhone and iPad, tap the + button, and type in what they need. On the Apple Watch, they can just open the app, scroll down down on the main screen, tap “Add Workout”, choose “just say it,” and describe what they want.

SmartGym + Siri AI

SmartGym 8 also leverages the new Siri AI, introduced in today’s 2027 OS updates. Here’s Abras:

SmartGym now integrates more deeply with Siri, making routines, exercises, equipment, muscle groups, schedules, and other training information accessible through natural voice requests. Siri can surface relevant SmartGym information directly and take you to the corresponding content when needed.

Users can now also start SmartGym workout sessions directly from Siri, in addition to controlling an active workout with commands such as “Next exercise in SmartGym,” or “Log set in SmartGym.”

With SmartGym’s data accessible to Siri, users can also ask questions such as “Which routines do I have in SmartGym this week?” or “Show me my dumbbell workouts in SmartGym,” and the app’s integration will not only surface the relevant information but also provide rich visual results right from the Siri interface.

This integration also works for specific session information, such as “Show my Heart Rates in SmartGym,” and even for exercise creation.

Users can also use the new Siri AI to create entirely new sessions by typing in or dictating a workout plan in natural language. Then, Siri AI and SmartGym will handle the rest, creating and organizing a new training routine based on the prompt.

Finally, SmartGym 8 also leverages Siri’s new on-screen awareness feature, which can be really helpful during gym sessions. Users can simply ask Siri to identify something on the screen, answer questions about it, or “Open the third routine on the screen,” and they can jump in without touching their device. Users can also start from an image, which is great for when they receive a written plan from their personal trainers.

Other tidbits

There’s plenty more in SmartGym 8. That includes:

Exercise Questions with images: SmartGym can now feed exercise execution images into Apple’s on-device Foundation Models to provide better and more descriptive answers about individual movements.

Resizable UI: The app’s interface now adapts more dynamically across different window sizes, orientations, and display shapes, getting the app ready for the new iPhone Duo.

More Liquid Glass: SmartGym has expanded its Liquid Glass design across more parts of the app, including its segmented controls, muscle group picker, alerts, and duration timer.

title: OpenAI buys smartphone camera maker Glass Imaging for $300 million, report says
snippet: Glass Imaging was founded by a pair of former Apple engineers who previously led the team that developed Apple's Portrait Mode.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

1:44 PM PDT · September 14, 2026

Image Credits:YIN WENJIE / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

OpenAI has bought smartphone camera maker Glass Imaging in a deal worth over $300 million, according to a report from The Wall Street Journal. The company, founded in 2019 and based in Los Altos, California, had previously raised about $30 million in funding from investors.

Glass Imaging was founded by Ziv Attar and Tom Bishop, a pair of former Apple engineers who previously led the team that developed Apple’s Portrait Mode. This background directly informs the work they now do at Glass Imaging, where they use AI to overcome the physical size constraints of smartphone cameras. Rather than using AI to edit a photo after it’s been taken, Glass Imaging uses neural networks to learn about individual camera systems — like the different cameras on various smartphone models — to yield better images from the moment the shutter clicks.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The ChatGPT maker is rumored to be working on its own hardware, like smartphones, earbuds, and AI companion devices. 

In 2025, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and famed Apple designer Jony Ive revealed that they had been working together on a device startup called io, when OpenAI bought Ive’s company for $6.5 billion.

For my entire IT career, software updates have operated on a predictable schedule. IT administrators have been conditioned to build workflows around quarterly point releases or monthly patching cycles (Patch Tuesday). However, as AI tools become very proficient at automatically discovering software vulnerabilities, threat actors are moving faster than ever before. With that being said, I very much miss 18th-month macOS/OS X releases.

We are rapidly entering an era in which software updates will look less like traditional operating system updates and more like continuous cloud updates. To survive this shift, IT teams must understand the three prongs of modern patch management.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

Prong 1: Re-educating the end user

The first pillar of this new world has to center completely on user experience and education. End users will have to accept a much more aggressive update approach. For years, users have treated operating system updates as optional annoyances that can be deferred until the last possible minute. In an era where zero-day vulnerabilities can be weaponized in just a few hours, that behavior is a massive liability. We might be entering an era in which zero-day issues occur almost monthly.

IT departments must prepare their workforces for frequent, mandatory interruptions. Much like applications such as Zoom or web browsers, which update constantly in the background, operating systems will require similar frequency of updates. Employees must understand that short-term disruption to their immediate productivity is a necessary trade-off to prevent data breaches for their organization.

Prong 2: Shrinking IT deployment windows

The second prong places an immense operational burden directly on IT deployment teams. Historically, an administrator might take 90 days to test a major operating system update against corporate applications before pushing it to production fleets. That timeline is completely dead, and I think 90 days might turn into 9 days or even 9 hours. 

Testing windows must shrink from months to weeks, days, or even hours, depending on the severity of the threat found. IT teams will need to lean heavily on device management tools to enforce compliance rules instantly. If a critical patch drops, administrators might need to prepare to automatically lock any device that remains unpatched by the end of the week or the end of the day, forcing the update before the user can resume work.

There might also need to be a distinction for different classes of employees as well. Developers with privileged access might need to see shorter windows than those in roles without it. 

Prong 3: The operating system architecture burden

The final prong lies squarely on the shoulders of the operating system vendors themselves. Google had a massive advantage when designing ChromeOS because they built a cloud-first platform from the ground up to support silent, background updates with near-instantaneous reboots. I manage 100s of Chromebooks, and it’s incredible how they stay up to date. Apple and Microsoft are carrying decades of legacy desktop architecture originally optimized for physical media installation. 

Apple has made significant strides here with declarative device management and Rapid Security Responses, enabling smaller security fixes to be installed without massive downtime. However, a standard macOS point release can still take 20 minutes of install time. Apple must continue to re-engineer the update process so that reboots happen seamlessly and, perhaps most importantly, application state is perfectly restored upon login, so users do not lose their active workspace layouts. I will say, Apple is light-years ahead of Microsoft, though. I’ve had Macs major releases (Ventura) behind and I can get them up to date with round of updates/reboot. I’ve had Windows 11 PCs that come out of the box, which take 4-5 rounds of reboots, random updates fail, and then you still have firmware updates on top of that.

9to5Mac’s take

The acceleration of security threats because AI means that patch management can no longer be a secondary task handled on a very predictable schedule. It must become a core, continuous discipline. In Apple environments, the infrastructure to support this is already being delivered through declarative device management technology. The technology exists, but IT leaders must shift their organizational mindsets to keep pace with modern threats. If you make the update process too slow or too painful, your users will fight it, and in the AI era, a delayed patch is an invitation for a breach. Apple has some work to do, though. More updates are needed across macOS and iOS without requiring a reboot, and it’s not going to be easy for Apple to retool how they work.

title: Report: iPhone price hike ‘better than feared,’ iPhone Duo to drive demand for the cycle
snippet: In an investor note seen by 9to5Mac, analyst Jeff Pu noted that while this week’s iPhone price hike was better than feared, the iPhone Duo is still likely to drive demand for the cycle, as early consumer interest appears strong. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In an investor note seen by 9to5Mac, analyst Jeff Pu noted that while this week’s iPhone price hike was better than feared, the iPhone Duo is still likely to drive demand for the cycle, as early consumer interest appears strong. Here are the details.

Pu sees iPhone 18 Pro uncertainty, iPhone Duo upside

According to GF Securities’ Jeff Pu, Apple’s $100 price hike for the new iPhone 18 Pro models came in below market expectations, which had pegged it at the $200–250 range.

He noted, however, that “the iPhone 18 series [will] likely face margin pressure, alongside limited hardware upgrades,” adding that the analysis company remains “cautious on the iPhone 18 Pro product cycle.”

When it comes to the iPhone Duo, Pu said the $1,999 device came in at the low end of the expected $2,000–2,500 price range and that he expects Apple to ship 7 million units through the end of the year.

From the analyst note:

For 2H26, we expect the iPhone 18 family to be supported by iPhone Duo (~7m units), while we see uncertainty around demand for iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max and the impact on margin. Consumer interest in iPhone Duo appears strong, driven by Apple’s first major form-factor innovation in years and a differentiated large-screen experience, thus we view iPhone Duo as a key demand driver for the iPhone 18 family and see post-launch order lead time and supply-chain build revisions as key indicators to watch.

Pu set a “hold” recommendation for Apple’s stock, defining the iPhone 18 series as a modest cycle, with its potential margin pressure and limited hardware upgrades “partially offset by the support of iPhone Duo.”

Under GF Securities’ rating system, a “Hold” implies expected relative stock performance of between -10% and 10%.

Finally, Pu shared GF Securities’ iPhone build forecast for the fourth quarter of 2026, which calls for 57 million iPhone 18-series units and 76 million iPhones overall, down 7% from the year-ago quarter:

title: Superhuman acquires YC-backed notetaker Fathom as productivity platforms push for agentic work
snippet: The notetaker offers a generous free plan, and that has resulted in over 400,000 monthly active users. The company said that over 1 million people have recorded meetings until now.
fullText:
Superhuman is joining the cadre of productivity platforms launching notetakers — but rather than building one internally, it is acquiring Y Combinator-backed Fathom.

AI-powered productivity platforms aim to automate work. Typically, that automation is triggered when a user types prompts and creates workflows. It would be even better, however, if AI could proactively start work, and for that, the topics and action items discussed in meetings are key. Hence the desire by Superhuman and similar platforms to move into notetaking.

To date, Fathom, which was founded in 2020, has raised over $30 million in funding, and it was valued at $94 million in 2024, according to data from PitchBook. Its investors include Zoom Apps Fund, Telescope Partners, BoxOne Ventures, Character Capital, and Maven Ventures. Its cap table also includes individuals such as Reddit CEO Steve Huffman, former Twitch CEO Emmett Shear, and Cruise co-founder Kyle Vogt.

The notetaker offers a generous free plan, and that has resulted in over 400,000 monthly active users. The company said that over 1 million people have recorded meetings until now. 

TechCrunch learned that earlier this year, Superhuman tested a notetaker internally with select users, but eventually chose to acquire a finished product to integrate with its productivity suite, with AI at the center. Shishir Mehrotra, Superhuman’s CEO, acknowledged this; he said that in the process of testing, the company realized how hard it is to create a notetaker.

“We’ve been working internally on this area for a while as well. I think it greatly increased our confidence in the demand in this category. It also becomes very clear how deep the products in this category are and how much you need to build. A lot of these products make the job feel really easy, but it’s actually quite tricky to do a great job in all parts [of meeting recording],” Mehrotra told TechCrunch over a call.

Mehrotra said that he was impressed with some of the technical intricacies built by the Fathom team, but didn’t elaborate on which ones. He did tease that with a notetaker, Superhuman can work on surfacing meeting context in real time.

Competition in the meeting notetaker space is intense, and startups like Granola, Read AI, and new entrant Wispr have raised millions of dollars to aid that growth. Despite having a healthy customer base or revenue run rate, venture-backed notetakers are feeling the heat from the market to do more than just notetaking. Some of these factors did matter in Superhuman acquiring Fathom, while Fathom’s CEO Richard White said that Superhuman’s 40 million user base was a good opportunity to reach users at scale.

“The reach of Superhuman is massive. I have always thought about M&A in terms of speed of building a product that everyone uses, and a part of that comes down to distribution. If we were to operate Fathom as a stand-alone company, we would have to build a lot of things that are already in the Superhuman platform,” he said.

On the platform front, Superhuman already has an email client, a docs app, a calendar, a database solution, and a newly launched AI agent builder platform. With a meeting notetaker in the middle, Superhuman can draft emails, update data entries, schedule follow-up meetings, and have AI agents start work and extract insights from meeting data.

snippet: While we’re still waiting on Samsung’s first Android XR glasses to arrive, an update on the first pair with a color display has found its way online, hinting at a launch sometime towards the end of next year. more…
fullText:
While we’re still waiting on Samsung’s first Android XR glasses to arrive, an update on the first pair with a color display has found its way online, hinting at a launch sometime towards the end of next year.

The Elec reports that Samsung has requested new microdisplays for future smart glasses, offering a color display. “Performance and price” are still both under consideration as Samsung Display works to deliver the needed form factor, with “ultra-small panels” around 0.2-inches or less. 

A monocular or binocular design is apparently undecided. Most initial prototypes that Google and Samsung have shown off have a monocular design, having just one display over a single eye, but a binocular design would have advantages such as being able to display 3D content. 

Samsung’s first Android XR glasses will not have a display, instead delivering a form factor similar to Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses with just a camera and open-ear headphones. Designs from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster have both been shown off, but an exact launch timeline hasn’t been confirmed yet.
