title: Gentler Streak and The Outsiders’ iOS 27 updates add Siri AI, onscreen awareness support, more
snippet: The unstoppable team at Gentler Stories is out today with updates to both of its exercise-tracking apps, taking advantage of the new Siri AI and other capabilities introduced with iOS 27. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
The unstoppable team at Gentler Stories is out today with updates to both of its exercise-tracking apps, taking advantage of the new Siri AI and other capabilities introduced with iOS 27. Here are the details.

Gentler Streak and The Outsiders get iOS 27 updates

Gentler Streak is without a doubt the app I’ve used most to track my performance, exercises, and especially recovery since I took up running and working out a few years ago.

Since joining 9to5Mac, I’ve had the opportunity of getting to know the people behind Gentler Stories, and it quickly became clear why Gentler Streak and its younger sibling, The Outsiders, are among the best fitness apps out there. The amount of love and care that goes into both apps is inspiring, and it quickly shows when you use them.

So it came as no surprise that both apps were updated today, allowing users to take advantage of some of the new features introduced with iOS 27 from day one.

With iOS 27 now available, Gentler Streak 5.13 and The Outsiders 1.8 can take advantage of the new App Intents capabilities, letting users ask the new Siri AI for health and fitness information from either app without having to open it first.

Additionally, both apps now support Siri’s new onscreen awareness capabilities, allowing the assistant to understand what users are looking at in the app and provide additional context about things like workout summaries, health charts, and other training data.

Here’s Gentler Stories’ CEO Katarina Lotrič on today’s updates:

Ask Siri for your daily health and fitness update (no need to open the app): check your training and health stats by asking Siri a question related to your health and fitness. Always make sure to include the app’s name to your prompt.

Gentler Streak: You can ask about today’s workouts, activity status, Go Gentler daily workout suggestions, daily body metrics, or last night’s sleep. (e.g., “Show today’s workouts in Gentler Streak”)

The Outsiders: You can ask about your training readiness, today’s workouts, daily body metrics, or last night’s sleep data. (e.g., “Training Readiness in The Outsiders?”)

Ask Siri for more context (when in the app): Open either of our two apps, go to a workout summary, a health chart, or a feature that’s unclear, and ask Siri to explain what’s on your screen. On-screen awareness turns Siri into an always available guide that can help you understand the app and your training better.

The update also introduces a new on-device, AI-powered workout title suggestion feature, which offers more descriptive names for recorded workouts while still letting users choose their own.

They also include a refreshed set of app icons, which, alongside the app’s own interfaces, further adopt the Liquid Glass look on both Gentler Streak and the Outsiders.

Finally, both apps now “automatically adjust to fit any screen size or position,” making them iPhone Duo-ready and better adapting to different iPad window sizes.

title: What execs and politicians are saying about slowing down AI development
snippet: Dario Amodei kicked off a flood of statements over the past few days about AI safety by publishing a long essay titled "We Must Pace the Frontier" detailing why AI development should be slowed down. Other AI leaders and politicians are speaking out in favor of or opposing his points, and we've compiled some of them here. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei Amodei's Saturday morning essay outlined three steps for pacing AI development: embedded third-party evaluators that can verify if a company is adhering to safety practices and commitments and report incidents, coordination between frontier AI companies in democratic countries on standards and li … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Dario Amodei kicked off a flood of statements over the past few days about AI safety by publishing a long essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier” detailing why AI development should be slowed down. Other AI leaders and politicians are speaking out in favor of or opposing his points, and we’ve compiled some of them here.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei

Amodei’s Saturday morning essay outlined three steps for pacing AI development: embedded third-party evaluators that can verify if a company is adhering to safety practices and commitments and report incidents, coordination between frontier AI companies in democratic countries on standards and limits, and global coordination between democratic governments and authoritarian governments on pacing AI development “to the extent this is possible.” Amodei said Anthropic is “unilaterally committing to the first of these steps.”

However, Amodei noted that pacing “does not mean halting model training or technical progress, ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this.”

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman

“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman said shortly after Amodei posted about his essay on X. “This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.” Altman also committed to having independent evaluators at the company, calling it a “great idea.”

On Sunday, Altman said OpenAI welcomes “a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI.” He added that OpenAI hopes other companies “learn from our approaches and propose their own; we think shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety will lead to better outcomes.” Like Amodei, Altman also said that “When we talk about “pacing”, we do not mean “stopping”, noting that progress should be “slower than it otherwise could be.”

Altman also noted two ways that he thinks AI progress “could go very badly”: losing “control of the future to AI” and ending up “in a world with too much concentration of power,” which he said can be avoided by “walking a narrow middle path.”

Google DeepMind co-founder and chair Demis Hassabis

“Dario’s essay points towards the right path forward,” Hassabis said in reply to Amodei’s essay. “The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment.” Hassabis also pointed to a framework for an AI standards body he published in July.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk

“Dario is right,” Musk said, reposting Amodei’s essay.

US President Donald Trump

In a rambling Monday morning Truth Social post, Trump pushed back on the idea of an AI slowdown:

The only control or “guardrails” that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades! The Trump Administration has stopped AI “people” from doing bad, or potentially bad, “things,“ like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a “perfect little angel” - and we will continue to do so! We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies! There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so. Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE! Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

While taking a call from Trump onstage at an event and putting the president on speakerphone, where he said that “the robots will not be taking over,” Huang said that “We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race in America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people.”

US Vice President JD Vance

Vance said that he feels it’s a “little bit weird” that frontier AI tech companies are “kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them” and added that it “feels a little bit to me like a bit of a trojan horse.” He also pointed to the President saying that “we know the Chinese are engaged in this long term AI race against the United States.”

House Speaker Mike Johnson

As part of a Sunday interview with Jake Tapper on CNN, Johnson said that “I think the leaders and the providers of all these platforms… They need to come together in a meeting with us and sit down and figure out what the right balance is. We cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us. And that’s the challenge. It’s national security balanced with the immediate security of making sure the models are safe.” It’s unclear if or when this meeting might actually happen, but Johnson said he would do it “tomorrow.”

Senator Bernie Sanders

Sanders said he agrees with Wall Street Journal columnist and former Ronald Reagan speechwriter Peggy Noonan, who published an article titled “Pause AI for Humanity’s Sake.”

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg

“For Congress to just sit on its hands, for the White House to do nothing real, is something that is deeply dangerous to the American people and to the world,” Buttigieg said in an NBC News interview. “There need to be safeguards, there need to be rules, there need to be limits, there needs to be a kill switch on rogue AI.”

Former White House AI and crypto czar David Sacks

”Dario has written that we need to ‘pace the frontier,’ and Sam has agreed,” Sacks said in a long post on X. “People may be surprised by my response: go ahead.” Sacks also told them to “stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission” and “stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic.”

Former FTC Chair Lina Khan

”Law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products,” Khan said to kick off a long post on X. “We shouldn’t let discussions about new legal regimes distract from the fact that there’s no AI exemption from laws already on the books — a point @FTC emphasized repeatedly during my tenure.”

Former Vice President Kamala Harris

“We must responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development,” Harris said as part of a thread, adding that “A slowdown is critical in order to ensure AI serves the public interest.“

Former Meta Chief AI Scientist Yann LeCun

“Dario was already claiming that GPT2 was too dangerous to open source back in 2019,” LeCun said in a reply on X. “I made fun of them then. Everyone should make fun of them now.”

Update, September 14th: Added more statements.

title: Apple releases iOS 27 with Siri AI and these new iPhone features
snippet: iOS 27 is officially here. After a summer of beta testing, the free software update has arrived for everyone. It brings Siri AI, new Apple Intelligence features, more control over Liquid Glass, and improvements throughout the system. Here’s what’s new, which iPhones support it, and how to update. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is officially here. After a summer of beta testing, the free software update has arrived for everyone. It brings Siri AI, new Apple Intelligence features, more control over Liquid Glass, and improvements throughout the system. Here’s what’s new, which iPhones support it, and how to update.

How to install iOS 27

You can download iOS 27 by opening Settings → General → Software Update on your iPhone. Select the iOS 27 upgrade, then follow the onscreen instructions.

Before installing, back up your iPhone using iCloud or a computer. Apple also provides installation instructions if you need help.

You may need to swipe down on the page to reveal the iOS 27 update option.

Siri AI is the biggest new feature

With iOS 27, Apple introduces a more conversational assistant called Siri AI.

The new Siri can use personal context to find information across your messages, emails, photos, and other content.

It also understands onscreen information and supports more actions across apps. That means you can ask follow-up questions or request help with what you’re viewing.

A dedicated Siri app lets you revisit conversations and continue them across supported Apple devices. Meanwhile, Siri mode in Camera brings Visual Intelligence into the viewfinder so you can ask about things around you.

Write with Siri also helps you draft and revise text. In Messages and Mail, it can adapt to your writing style.

Which iPhones support Siri AI?

Siri AI and the new Apple Intelligence features require iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or an iPhone 16 model or later. iPhone Air and iPhone Duo also support Siri AI.

Liquid Glass gets more controls

iOS 27 adds a slider in Settings that lets you adjust Liquid Glass from clear to fully tinted. Apple also refines app icons and the system’s appearance.

Performance is another focus. Apple reports faster app launches, quicker loading of newly captured photos, and faster AirDrop transfers in its testing. Search improvements also aim to make results more useful in Spotlight, Photos, and Mail.

Photos and Safari gain new AI tools

On supported iPhones, Photos adds several editing options:

Spatial Reframing: Adjust a photo’s composition by virtually changing the camera position.

Extend: Expand an image beyond its original edges.

Clean Up: Remove larger objects with improved results.

Safari also gains automatic tab grouping by topic. In addition, Notify Me can monitor a webpage for changes, such as a price drop or an item returning to stock.

More iOS 27 features worth trying

	

Apple also detail several practical additions:

AirPods Custom EQ: Adjust audio to suit your preferences.

Separate alarm and timer volume: Set independent volume levels for alarms and timers.

Expanded parental controls: Approve new websites with Ask to Browse, set app schedules, and manage daily time allowances.

Communication Safety updates: Extend protections to images and videos containing gore or violence.

Call Context: Surface relevant information, such as a reservation number, during supported business calls.

Accessibility improvements: Expand capabilities in VoiceOver, Magnifier, Accessibility Reader, and Voice Control.

Read Apple’s full release notes for the detailed breakdown.

Which iOS 27 feature are you trying first? Let us know in the comments.

title: Nintendo Switch Owners Should Update Their Firmware After Security Exploit Discovered
snippet: The issue does not affect the Nintendo Switch 2.
fullText:
Owners of the original Nintendo Switch should patch a security exploit immediately, especially if they game in public. Nintendo announced the vulnerability (PDF) on Sept. 10, shortly after releasing its latest 23.0.0 firmware update.

The exploit applies only to original Nintendo Switch owners using the Send to Smartphone feature. This feature generates a QR code on the Switch that you can scan with a smartphone, letting you transfer game captures and screenshots directly to your phone. 

It also affects people playing Super Mario Kart: Home Circuit on the physical cartridge, as the game uses a QR code to establish a wireless link with nearby players. 

Should someone else scan the QR code before you, they can connect their device to your Switch and use the connection to run unauthorized code on your Switch or steal information stored on the game console. Since your account information is stored on your Switch, that’s information you don’t want in the hands of someone else. 

A Nintendo representative did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.

The exploit does not affect the Nintendo Switch 2. 

How to fix the problem

The fix is pretty simple. Nintendo released update 23.0.0 on Sept. 9, which fixes the exploit. It’s recorded as CVE-2026-82079, which is “a stock-based buffer overflow vulnerability” that lets attackers within wireless range execute code. It only affects the original Switch on firmware versions older than 23.0.0.

To update your Nintendo Switch, head to System Settings > System > System Update to apply the update. Follow any additional on-screen prompts to install the update. 

Nintendo says that those who can’t immediately update their firmware can avoid the issue by only using the Send to Smartphone feature at home, where attackers can’t see them, or by not playing Super Mario Kart: Home Circuit in public. The gaming giant also recommends not scanning any QR codes with any device that isn’t yours. 

People who only play games at home are protected from this exploit and don’t have to worry about it.

title: Apple extends free iPhone satellite access for another year
snippet: Apple is extending free access to its satellite features for existing iPhone users for another year, the company revealed in a footnote to its iPhone 18 Pro press release. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple is extending free access to its satellite features for existing iPhone users for another year, the company revealed in a footnote to its iPhone 18 Pro press release. Here are the details.

Apple confirms new extension

Apple first introduced satellite connectivity on the iPhone with the iPhone 14 lineup, initially offering Emergency SOS via satellite and the ability to share your location through Find My via satellite. At launch, Apple said access would be free for two years.

Since then, Apple has expanded its satellite offering with additional features, including Roadside Assistance via satellite and Messages via satellite. The company now collectively refers to these as its satellite features.

In November 2023, Apple extended free access to Emergency SOS via satellite by another year for existing iPhone 14 users. Last year, Apple again extended free access, this time covering its satellite features for existing iPhone 14 and iPhone 15 users.

This meant that without another extension, free access would have begun to expire for some users later this year. However, Apple revealed in a footnote to yesterday’s iPhone 18 Pro press release that it is extending free access for another year, now including existing iPhone 16 users as well.

From the press release:

When outside of cellular and Wi-Fi coverage, Apple’s groundbreaking satellite features help iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max users stay connected and get assistance when it matters most. Apple is extending free access to satellite features for an additional year for existing iPhone 14, iPhone 15, and iPhone 16 users. The free trial will be extended for iPhone 14, iPhone 15, and iPhone 16 users who have activated their device in a country that supports Apple’s satellite features prior to midnight PT on September 9. For satellite feature availability, visit support.apple.com/en-us/105097.

Since Apple gives buyers of new iPhones one year of free access to its satellite features, this means that users who buy the new iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo will get their own free year, while existing iPhone 14, iPhone 15, and iPhone 16 users covered by the extension will also get another year of free access.

To this day, Apple has not announced how much it plans to charge for its satellite features once the free access period ends. Given that these are potentially life-saving features, many speculate that Apple might ultimately keep at least some of them free, since charging users for access to emergency services could prove controversial.

Be that as it may, free access has been extended for another year. Whether this is the last extension, or we’ll be publishing a similar story again next year, remains to be seen.

Do you think Apple will ever charge for satellite access? Let us know in the comments.

title: Voicemod’s new pocket-friendly device brings real-time voice changing to your phone
snippet: Voicemod announced a new mobile device that expands the capabilities of the Voicemod Key dongle it launched in late 2024 as a way to bring the company's real-time voice changing tech to consoles. While the older Voicemod Key only used a smartphone as an interface between the company's mobile app and the Xbox, PlayStation, and Switch, the new Key Pocket can be used to change your voice or trigger sound effects while you're playing games, making calls, or streaming on Apple or Android mobile devices. The Voicemod Key Pocket is now available as a standalone device for $99.90 or as part of a $129.90 bundle that includes the hardware and a Voice … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Voicemod announced a new mobile device that expands the capabilities of the Voicemod Key dongle it launched in late 2024 as a way to bring the company’s real-time voice changing tech to consoles. While the older Voicemod Key only used a smartphone as an interface between the company’s mobile app and the Xbox, PlayStation, and Switch, the new Key Pocket can be used to change your voice or trigger sound effects while you’re playing games, making calls, or streaming on Apple or Android mobile devices.

The Voicemod Key Pocket is now available as a standalone device for $99.90 or as part of a $129.90 bundle that includes the hardware and a Voicemod Pro license. The extra $30 fee gets you lifetime access to the hundreds of voices created by the company and the thousands made by the community, the ability to create your own custom voices, and cloud syncing across multiple platforms without a subscription.

Although Voicemod first expanded outside the PC with the introduction of Voicemod Clips on iOS and Android in 2020, the mobile app could only be used to change your voice when recording short video or audio clips you could share afterward. Privacy restrictions on mobile operating systems prevent apps from altering microphone audio and sending it to other apps.

The Voicemod Key Pocket doesn’t change that. The pocket-friendly device, which can stick to the back of phones or tablets that support magnetic accessories, functions as an external audio bridge. Audio from a wired or Bluetooth microphone connected to the Pocket is altered by Voicemod’s mobile app and then made available to other apps, like Fortnite, Roblox, Discord, or the apps you use for making phone or video calls, through a short USB-C cable connected to your mobile device.

With the Pro license, the app provides access to over 200 voices created by Voicemod (instead of just a small selection of constantly rotating voices for free) and more than 76,000 additional options created by the community. The Pocket features six programmable buttons that can be used to quickly swap between voices or trigger short soundboard clips, a dedicated mute button, and a customizable glowing LED dial for altering voices or adjusting volume. Like the Voicemod Key, the Key Pocket can also be used as a voice changer for the latest generation of consoles, including the Switch 2 and recent versions of the Meta Quest headset.

title: Volvo’s plug-in hybrid XC60 and XC90 can really go the distance
snippet: Most plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEV) today get an average of around 30-50 miles of battery-only range: decent, but not mind-blowing. With hybrid sales dominating the market today, Volvo is out to prove that its PHEVs can push the limits of what's possible. Today, the Swedish automaker revealed the updated PHEV versions of its popular XC60 and XC90 SUVs are its first "long range plug-in hybrids," delivering class-leading ranges of 78 miles and 73 miles, respectively. That's more than double the electric range of previous PHEV variants. The numbers are still preliminary and based on EPA testing standards. But if confirmed, they would … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Most plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEV) today get an average of around 30–50 miles of battery-only range: decent, but not mind-blowing. With hybrid sales dominating the market today, Volvo is out to prove that its PHEVs can push the limits of what’s possible.

Today, the Swedish automaker revealed the updated PHEV versions of its popular XC60 and XC90 SUVs are its first “long range plug-in hybrids,” delivering class-leading ranges of 78 miles and 73 miles, respectively. That’s more than double the electric range of previous PHEV variants. The numbers are still preliminary and based on EPA testing standards. But if confirmed, they would make Volvo’s PHEVs “the longest electric range of any plug-in hybrids available in the American market,” the automaker claims.

Volvo took a page from its all-electric vehicle design by integrating the battery directly in the floor of both vehicles for improved efficiency. The batteries are also higher capacity — 41.2 kWh (37.9 kWh usable) for both — and able to send more energy to the motors, which are also more powerful.

1/3

Of course, those batteries are just dead weight if owners forget to charge them — which tends to happen with a lot of plug-in hybrids. Hybrid owners often neglect to charge, thanks to the gas tank that continues to power their vehicle even with a dead battery. Still, the higher capacity batteries in the XC60 and XC90 are sure to appeal to a lot of car shoppers who may still like the sound of increased range even if they don’t exactly plan on taking full advantage of it.

The XC60 is getting new styling to bring it inline with Volvo’s new design language. That includes an upgraded grille, redesigned front bumper, hood, front wings, rear bumper, tailgate, new wheel designs, and a refined “Thor’s Hammer” LED headlight light signature. Like the redesigned XC40, the XC60 also has a more expansive driver assist that includes Automatic Emergency Steering and Braking, collision prevention, and a door-opening cyclist alert.

The addition of Google’s Gemini chatbot as the new voice assistant rounds everything out. Volvo was one of the first automakers to adopt Google’s software for its infotainment systems, so naturally that now includes Gemini.

Production on the XC60 and XC90 begins late Fall 2026, with customer deliveries scheduled to begin in early 2027. Volvo is hoping that a boost in hybrid sales can help fund its future pure EV models, like the EX50, EX60, and new affordable model that will replace the EX30.

title: Apple Home’s new security camera features cost as much as $60 a month
snippet: New Apple Intelligence features for HomeKit cameras start at $10 a month and go up to $60. | Image: The Verge With the public release of iOS 27 and tvOS 27, Apple Home is getting an injection of Apple Intelligence - but you'll have to pay more for it. Apple Intelligence for Home brings AI-powered video summaries to HomeKit Secure Video, so you can get short text descriptions of who and what compatible security cameras saw, along with the clip. It also adds a new video search feature and the ability to stitch footage from multiple cameras into one clip, making it easier to keep an eye on what's happening around your home without scrolling through footage. But to get these features, you'll need to pay $9.99 a month for the 2TB iCloud Plus plan (or $ … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
With the public release of iOS 27 and tvOS 27, Apple Home is getting an injection of Apple Intelligence — but you’ll have to pay more for it.

Apple Intelligence for Home brings AI-powered video summaries to HomeKit Secure Video, so you can get short text descriptions of who and what compatible security cameras saw, along with the clip. It also adds a new video search feature and the ability to stitch footage from multiple cameras into one clip, making it easier to keep an eye on what’s happening around your home without scrolling through footage.

AI-generated video summaries provide text descriptions of what a camera sees.

But to get these features, you’ll need to pay $9.99 a month for the 2TB iCloud Plus plan (or $39.95 a month for an Apple One Premier subscription) — and that’s just for one camera. According to an Apple support page, to add Apple Intelligence to a second camera, you’ll have to pay $29.99 a month for the 6TB plan. For up to five cameras, it’s a whopping $59.99 a month for the 12TB plan. No word on whether you can add more than five cameras. (Recordings from HomeKit-connected cameras don’t count toward your storage quota.)

That’s way too expensive. While the improved video features are useful — I’ve been testing them in beta and have been impressed — they’re not good enough to justify that big a price jump.

HomeKit Secure Video has always been behind a paywall, but it started at a very reasonable $1 a month. That’s for the 50GB iCloud Plus plan, which includes recorded footage from one camera, plus smart alerts and facial recognition. For more cameras, you bump up to 2TB / $9.99 a month (up to five), and 6TB / $29.99 a month or higher for unlimited cameras. But the cost for the Apple Intelligence features is a huge increase.

1/4Apple Intelligence requires the 2TB $9.99 a month plan, for more cameras you need to upgrade to 6TB or 12TB.

I currently pay $40 a month for Apple One Premier, which includes 2TB of iCloud storage and gets me HomeKit Secure Video support for five cameras. With the new pricing tier, I keep those benefits and now get Apple Intelligence on one camera. But to get it on all five cameras, I’d need to pay an additional $60 a month. That’s $720 a year, for a total of $1,200.

Amazon’s Ring and Google Nest charge around $20 a month for subscription tiers that include similar AI-powered features for their cameras, and both companies offer more features than Apple currently does. An iCloud Plus plan does include storage for photos, files, and device backups, and higher plans may get you higher limits for Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features, but Apple hasn’t released any details about that.

The good news is that none of this changes what you get with the standard HomeKit Secure Video today, and the new software releases have added under-the-hood upgrades that improve speed and reliability, plus the service now supports 4K video resolution. The change only applies if you want the new Apple Intelligence video features. But while Apple Intelligence feels like a significant improvement for Apple Home, at these prices, the value just isn’t there.

title: ClickFix attacks are tricking Mac and Windows users into hacking themselves
snippet: If you clicked on a fake HBO Max ad on Reddit in the past week, you might have fallen victim to a rising "ClickFix" security threat.
fullText:
If you clicked on an HBO Max ad on Reddit over the past week, you might want to check your computer for malware.

These so-called “ClickFix” attacks have quickly become one of the rising cybersecurity threats of 2026, and they’re getting both sneakier and compromising people’s devices with greater frequency. Until recently, ClickFix attacks were a rarity, capitalizing on people searching the web for quick tech fixes. They have since evolved into a massive international effort to hack into people’s computers.

The attacks involve fake websites, or legitimate websites that have been hacked, which display a message that appears to look like a CAPTCHA or an anti-bot checkbox. Once clicked, a prompt appears asking the user to perform a “check” to proceed, which gives instructions to copy and paste a string of text into the user’s Windows command prompt or Mac Terminal app. 

As soon as the user hits return, they unwittingly and instantly install info-stealing malware on their computer, capable of immediately stealing their passwords, access to their logged-in accounts, and crypto wallets. Since the user is working in the computer’s terminal, which lets them interact directly with the operating system using text-based commands, many of these attacks evade antivirus and security defense tools.

Security researchers now say that the latest ClickFix campaign they’ve seen involved hackers posting fake ads on Reddit, linking to a page that looks like HBO Max but contains a ClickFix lure that tricks people into hacking themselves. The hackers compromised the official HBO Max’s account on Reddit that was then used to post hundreds of fake but real-looking adverts to the news-sharing site, according to security researchers at Hudson Rock and ADAMnetworks, and a thread on Reddit’s cybersecurity subreddit.

It’s unclear how many people clicked on these fake ads or how many were ultimately compromised as a result. Warner Brothers Discovery, which owns HBO, did not respond to a request for comment.

Reddit told TechCrunch it “recently learned that an HBO Max account authorized to run advertisements on Reddit was compromised and used to run ads containing malicious links,” and that the company locked the account and removed the ads. When asked, Reddit did not say how many users were targeted or clicked the malicious ads.

While it’s typical for developers to run one-line snippets of code in their computer’s terminal, it’s less common for regular users to use the Command Prompt or PowerShell in Windows, or the Terminal in macOS. Companies that run fleets of Windows computers can block access to these features across the entire domain to prevent them from being exploited, per security researcher Kevin Beaumont.

As noted by Ars Technica, a tool for Mac users called BlockBlock can also defend against attacks that try to trick Apple users into hacking themselves.

title: Apple researchers unveil SimpleDesign, a new AI model for protein design
snippet: In a new study, Apple researchers detail SimpleDesign, a streamlined AI model that can jointly generate protein sequences and structures. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a new study, Apple researchers detail SimpleDesign, a streamlined AI model that can jointly generate protein sequences and structures. Here are the details.

A bit of context

Last September, Apple researchers published a study titled “SimpleFold: Folding Proteins is Simpler than You Think,” which detailed a streamlined approach to predicting a protein’s 3D structure from its amino acid sequence.

In a nutshell, SimpleFold uses a flow-matching model to generate a protein’s 3D structure directly from its amino acid sequence.

We explained flow matching in more detail here, but the short of it is that the technique starts with a noisy, random basis and learns a relatively direct path toward the final result. That contrasts with diffusion models, which typically work by iteratively removing noise until they reach the final output.

Both techniques are most commonly (or at least historically) associated with image generation, although researchers (including those at Apple) have also explored diffusion models for text and code generation.

Back to SimpleFold, Apple basically paired flow matching with general-purpose Transformer blocks (commonly used in text generation), allowing the model to avoid some of the more computationally expensive techniques typically used by protein-folding models, such as DeepMind’s famous AlphaFold.

Now, Apple researchers have unveiled SimpleDesign, which applies the same push toward simpler, general-purpose architectures explored with SimpleFold to the broader problem of protein design, rather than just predicting a protein’s 3D structure.

SimpleDesign

As Apple’s researchers explain in a new study titled “SimpleDesign: A Joint Model for Protein Sequence and Structure Codesign”:

Existing models often rely on a multi-stage training process where autoencoders that tokenize data into latent representations are trained in a first stage. Secondly, a generative model is trained on the latent representation of the autoencoder(s), i.e. generative modeling in a latent space. We hypothesize that this multi-stage training is not necessary to obtain performant co-design models and thus present SimpleDesign, an effective multi-modal protein design model trained directly in the data space.

In other words, while many existing protein design models rely on a multi-stage process, SimpleDesign learns to generate amino acid sequences and continuous 3D structures in a single end-to-end training process.

Many current protein co-design models work as follows: first, they train a separate model to convert protein structures into discrete representations, or “tokens.” Then, they train a generative model to work with those representations to generate new protein sequences and structures.

SimpleDesign skips that intermediate step, learning directly from paired amino acid sequences and 3D coordinates rather than first compressing protein structures into a separate tokenized representation.

The way Apple researchers trained SimpleDesign is quite interesting.

They started with more than 2 million protein sequence-and-structure pairs, taken primarily from the AFESM dataset, which combines predicted structures from the AlphaFold Database and additional samples.

During training, they corrupted both parts of each pair: while amino acids in the sequence were randomly hidden behind masked tokens, the corresponding 3D structure also had noise added to it.

The researchers would also vary the extent to which each side was scrambled. If the sequence was mostly intact but the structure was heavily corrupted, the task resembled protein folding, and the model had to recover a structure from a known sequence.

By contrast, if the structure was mostly intact but the sequence was heavily masked, it resembled inverse folding. The model then had to generate a sequence capable of producing a given structure.

And when both were partially scrambled, the model learned to work on the two problems simultaneously, effectively training it for protein co-design.

According to the study, SimpleDesign delivered competitive results across protein co-design, structure generation, and sequence generation benchmarks, despite using a much simpler training pipeline.

The researchers also found that SimpleDesign could generate plausible protein structures, and that the amino acid sequences it produced were generally as good as or better than those generated by most competing multimodal models.

Finally, the researchers noted that SimpleDesign’s results are still limited to computer-based evaluations, since the generated proteins were not experimentally tested to confirm that they would actually fold, function, or behave safely in actual biological systems.

Still, the results were quite promising, and the entire study (which naturally goes much more in depth on SimpleDesign’s architecture, training process, benchmarks, and results) is well worth a look.

title: Yes, the iPhone Duo Is a First-Generation Phone. That’s Why You Should Get One if You Can
snippet: Despite its price, more people who don’t use tech the way I do should own this iPhone.
fullText:
You take a risk when you buy the first version of something to ever exist, even when it’s made by a company with a history as well-documented as Apple’s. The new iPhone Duo looks cool, with its passport-style hinge and massive displays, but buying it is still a risk. You’re spending at least $2,000 on something you’ll use for multiple hours every day over at least the next 12 months, which is enough to give just about anyone a moment of pause to check in mentally and make sure this is the right decision.

The risk is real, I get it. Do it anyway, and be loud about it.

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Apple is nowhere near the first to make a foldable phone, but this is the first iPhone that will bend (more than once, at least). That’s an interesting place to be, due largely to the folks who tend to own iPhones. Samsung is in its seventh year of releasing foldables, and I maybe see one or two of them in the wild when I wander major cities or busy airports. The folks who have them love them, and they’re happy to tell their friends about the cool things these phones can do, but the audience is largely early adopters, comfortable with things that aren’t fully baked. 

Feedback from someone who isn’t tech-obsessed will always be more valuable to Apple than to a lot of its competitors. Features will be created and retired from that feedback, and it will eventually appear on most other folding phones.

My favorite example of this is actually another Apple product, the Watch. The first Apple Watch had some fitness features, but was largely focused on the idea that you could leave your phone behind because that’s what the competition was doing already. Instead of trying to replicate your phone in watch form, right down to the tiny keyboard seen on other smartwatches at the time, Apple focused on its fitness tracking and health monitoring features. They quickly became the most popular.

By the time the third-gen Apple Watch was announced, GPS and cellular features were now being shown off as a way to make those fitness features better. The Watch was no longer about replacing your phone. Now that we’re at Apple Watch Gen 12, fitness is basically all anyone talks about.

The iPhone Duo can be propped half-open to easily watch movies and access controls.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The next six months are going to be important for the future of Apple’s contribution to the foldable phone market, because the audience response will help shape the next iPhone Duo. Popular third-party apps will become native features, accessories will be made to address situations that haven’t happened yet and current features will be copied in every direction. It benefits everyone if the majority of the folks providing early feedback and getting excited about new ways to use this phone are outside of the standard group of IT folks, business execs on weekly flights or whoever is going to watch that front screen for 44 hours.

Grab one, if you can afford it. Watch Netflix on it and talk about how that experience could be better. Use your favorite apps side by side and see if it’s easy or intuitive for you to figure out on your own. Be an early adopter, and this time next year a lot more people will feel like the Duo was made with them in mind.

title: Comu’s Action Pro is a great meeting recorder that struggles to justify its AI premium
snippet: As my house becomes increasingly strewn with the detritus of parenting, I’ve made the inverse effort to eliminate excess, physical and digital, from my life. As much as it is about control, it’s also about mental health; I already use my phone too much, so adding yet another thing to the backpack, to the pocket, feels anything but additive. more…
fullText:
As my house becomes increasingly strewn with the detritus of parenting, I’ve made the inverse effort to eliminate excess, physical and digital, from my life. As much as it is about control, it’s also about mental health; I already use my phone too much, so adding yet another thing to the backpack, to the pocket, feels anything but additive.

But I’m also aware of the single-use gadget’s pull, increasingly powerful precisely because people are relying too much on their phones. Digicams to augment overly-processed smartphone photos. Writing tablets that feel like paper without the waste. Smart rings and health trackers to reduce notification overload.

And so it is with a product like the Comu Action Pro, a standalone note-taking gadget that attempts to turn a simple idea into something indispensable.

Pixel owners are likely well aware of the superlative built-in Recorder app that’s been around for years, adding features like real-time transcription and translation as it’s matured. The current app is about all you could want from a piece of software that leverages a phone’s built-in microphones.

	

It was with this framing that I undertook the review of a novel gadget category: the AI voice recorder. I’m not entirely unfamiliar with it: I’ve used early versions of Plaud’s NotePin and Note devices in the past, but never for long enough to feel acquainted with them. In response, I wanted to spend enough time with the Comu Action Pro to understand where and how it fits into my life, and why one may feel justified in spending the $180 it currently costs instead of just using the phone they already have in their pocket.

First, the basics: at a thickness of 7mm, it’s a svelte mixture of aluminum and plastic that’s designed to stick magnetically to the back of a compatible phone, like an iPhone or Pixel. (The box comes with a couple of circular magnetic stickers for devices without built-in MagSafe support.) That said, it’s nowhere close to the 3mm dimensions of the Plaud Note and Note Pro. But that additional girth comes with a few benefits: it fits a USB-C port, so you’re not forced to charge it with a proprietary magnetic cable that will almost certainly be missing when you need it most. And it carries a larger battery that pushes recording time to 70 hours, double that of the Plaud Note Pro.

The primary question I ask myself, and am asked by others, when I use the Comu Action Pro is, “Why?” Why do you need a separate piece of hardware when your phone will suffice, particularly in a world of inexpensive or free AI transcription services that can do most of the job? In short, it’s the passivity of it all; you can just leave the Action Pro running in the background whenever you’re going about your day to collect snippets of conversations, or covertly place it on a boardroom table to record a meeting.

The Action Pro has six far-field microphones that pick up voices from distances that phones are just not tuned for. That omnidirectional nature means the actual recordings sound thin and tinny, but the product is not the audio — it’s the data from the audio. Placing the Action Pro on the table in front of me next to my phone and recording the deliberately subdued tones of a conversation I was having showed the form factor’s inherent compromise; it picked up voices from the tables next to me, leading to audio that was basically unusable to listen to. Conversely, my Pixel 11 Pro did a great job isolating our two voices in the recording itself.

I was surprised, then, to discover the Action Pro transcribed our conversation with minimal errors. The company works with a number of AI vendors, including OpenAI and Google, and while it’s usually accurate, it made more errors than the competition.

It’s the “Action” in Comu’s Action Pro the company really wants to emphasize, and it’s what I believe has the largest potential — and the longest way to go to reach it. If you’ve ever used a cloud-based meeting recorder like Granola you’ll know that its primary job is to synthesize what it records into something compelling and useful, a summary that can lead to identifiable action items. From there you can ask it questions about the content or have it draft a follow-up email.

Comu’s Action Pro tries to go one step further by integrating with foundation models like Claude Opus 5 or GPT-5.6 Terra to turn those summaries into more than just emails; you can ask it to create a summary document or even a presentation, choosing from a number of predefined templates. All of this is done through the app, which is poorly designed, making for an awkward experience.

I’ll give you a small example: I had the Comu Action Pro record all 20 minutes of a YouTube video that was playing at a pretty comfortable volume from my Mac Mini’s thin but capable internal speaker. It was a video I watched doing research for this review, attempting to grasp the scope of the AI note taking market, since I’d really only ever heard of and used Plaud’s products.

As a baseline, I also used my Pixel 11 Pro’s Recorder app alongside a Plaud Note. All three were sitting four or so inches from the speaker and there was little ambient noise in the room. After the recording was finished, I compared the transcripts of each recorder for accuracy, and then delved into the post-production aspects of each product. For full transparency, here are links to both Comu’s and Plaud’s outputs from that recording:

Summaries are good on both, but Plaud’s are neater and better organized.

Plaud’s transcript is slightly more accurate.

Ironically, the Action Pro kept referring to Plaud as “Plot” throughout, though that can be traced to the word’s pronunciation by the host.

Plaud’s output included a mind map and a summary image, whereas Comu’s was text-only.

Comu’s custom documents and presentations are basic, hard to read, and rarely useful as standalone assets.

The Comu app is buggy and, in places, poorly translated into English.

The Comu web app is basically unusable in its current state.

The issue I keep returning to is that the Action Pro really only solves a real-world problem. While you can attach it to the back of the phone to record both sides of a conversation (with consent, of course), there’s no mechanism to record or sync web-based meetings. Plaud, being the more mature product, boasts a much better app, a usable web interface, and a desktop app that records and transcribes video calls, usage of which is included even in the free Starter plan.

Comu’s best features are also gated behind a subscription. Unlike Plaud, which provides access to most features for free but limits transcription minutes to 300 on the free Starter tier, Comulytic goes the other way, offering unlimited transcriptions indefinitely and putting its AI workflows, including translation and document generation, behind a $10/month paywall. Access to Anthropic’s Claude model is also limited to paid subscriptions.

Those are the actions meant to be solved by the dedicated AI button that sits above the record button which, when pressed, acts like a voice-powered agent for your work needs. Anything recorded when the button is pressed goes into a general ChatGPT-like stream, where the data source is the transcribed meeting notes. Unfortunately, that’s where the “Action” part of the Action Pro breaks down: the Comu agent is brittle, and doesn’t interface with other parts of the phone. 

For instance, there’s a “Schedule Tasks” prompt that Comu invites you to use, and tapping it pre-fills a number of templates, including “Schedule a deep work block for this week.” I completed the prompt and wrote “Schedule a deep work block for this Friday from 1 to 5 PM,” but at the moment the model isn’t able to connect to my external calendar. 

In fact, as of writing, every calendar- and task-based connection is listed as “Coming soon.” Once these connections are added, Comu’s offering may be more competitive, but given the proliferation of similar services like Gemini Spark, Meta Muse, Town, Poke, and many others, I’m doubtful that most users will be willing to shell out the monthly fee that Comu is asking for.

At its core, the Action Pro is a competent meeting transcriber with some impressive hardware and lackluster software that, at least right now, doesn’t justify its asking price. If you’re looking for something from the company that’s thinner, lighter, and cheaper, and still has some AI capabilities, Comu’s own Note Pro is a decent alternative at under $120. If you need something a bit more full-featured, including better web and desktop support, I’d go with something from Plaud.

					

A competent meeting recorder and digital note taker whose ambitions to be an AI project manager don’t quite work.

					

				

Pros

				

											

Great audio transcription quality

											

Good build quality

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

App is a mess

											

AI features are half-baked or missing entirely

											

AI features require a minimum $10/month subscription

Writing tablets that feel like paper without the waste. Smart rings and health trackers to reduce notification overload.

snippet: When Jensen Huang took a live call from Trump, some of us were more focused on the phone he used to take it.

Jensen Huang made headlines Monday at the All-In conference in LA when President Trump called him, live, onstage. But there was something else worth noting about his appearance. Huang, dressed in his now-signature alligator leather jacket, was handed a foldable phone to answer it.

Once he got Trump on speaker, the conversation turned to AI safety, and the two seemed to agree that mounting fears about AI equate to what Trump called a “hoax.” Trump argued that the real winners of the AI panic are China and “political people,” and that the technology is too big — “bigger than the internet,” he said — to slow down over. Nvidia’s business model depends largely on AI labs buying more chips, so downplaying existential risk is the only move if he cares about his company’s share price. title: The premium AirPods 5 are the best open-ear earbuds Apple has made
snippet: The AirPods 5 earbuds and case look identical to the AirPods 4. Apple … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
It’s almost a guarantee that the new version of a product will be, at best, the same price as the old one, and often (especially in the past couple years) more expensive. But that’s not what Apple did with the AirPods 5. The $149 AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case are $30 cheaper than the AirPods 4 with ANC they replace. They have slightly better active noise cancellation, and they’re the first non-Pro AirPods with volume controls on the stem. Apple has never made wireless earbuds that offer as much for so little, and they make the base AirPods 5, which are $20 cheaper but don’t have wireless charging or volume controls, pointless.

8

Verge Score

$149

The Good

Cheaper than the AirPods 4 with ANC

Improved sound

Volume swipe control

The Bad

Below-average battery life

Confusing naming convention

The AirPods 5, like all non-Pro AirPods, use an open-ear design, meaning they don’t have silicone ear tips to form a seal in your ear canal. Last generation, Apple offered two versions of the AirPods: one with active noise cancellation and one without. This time around, there are still two models. But both models of the AirPods 5 include active noise cancellation. They both also have adaptive audio and transparency mode, plus live translation with an iPhone 15 Pro or later, and are IP57 rated (up from IP54 on the AirPods 4). The main differences between the $129 AirPods 5 and the $149 AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case — aside from the wireless charging case and the annoyingly long name — are the volume controls, battery life, and 20 bucks.

That extra $20 is well worth it. The wireless charging case is nice (it isn’t MagSafe, but it does work with the magnetic Apple Watch charger). But the most important change is that they finally have swipe volume controls. That’s one thing that’s been missing from all non-Pro AirPods until now. Part of the convenience of wireless earbuds is that you can leave your phone in your pocket or bag, and omitting volume control on the earbuds themselves defeats the purpose. With the two models so close in price, I can’t understand why Apple even released the base AirPods 5.

The AirPods 5’s mesh screens are denser than the 4, naturally blocking more ambient sound.

Apple says that both models of the AirPods 5 have up to 50 percent better noise cancellation than the AirPods 4 with ANC, but the company doesn’t provide details about which frequencies are affected (we’ll have to wait for folks like SoundGuys to put them on their measurement rig). While the size and look of the AirPods remains the same, Apple redesigned the internal acoustic architecture, reworked the algorithm, and included denser mesh on the ports for slightly more passive attenuation (naturally reducing ambient noise), which helps achieve that ANC improvement. In my own subjective testing, I could hear minor benefits both with low-end airplane drones and when out at a busy restaurant picking up some burritos to go.

The AirPods 4 with ANC already delivered better noise-canceling than any other open-ear design I’ve heard (particularly clip earbuds), and the AirPods 5 do step that up. But don’t expect the kind of isolation you get from sealed earbuds like the AirPods Pro 3, which are often on sale for only $50 more.

The AirPods 5 (right) share the exterior design as the AirPods 4 (middle), and are inspired by the internal acoustic architecture of the AirPods Pro 3 (left).

Apple has always led the field with its transparency mode, but with the AirPods 5, there’s now barely any perceivable difference between transparency mode and not wearing the earbuds at all. With other earbuds, transparency mode generally boosts high-frequency ambient sounds a little, such as the sibilance of esses. Verge laptop reviewer Antonio Di Benedetto wore the new AirPods on a 5K run and found transparency mode to be preferable to ANC, as it gave great awareness without wind noise. It also never felt like the earbuds were in danger of falling out of his ears.

The redesigned internals also benefit the AirPods 5’s sound. There’s more bass response — something I felt the AirPods 4 were sorely lacking — and vocals have more clarity and aren’t as covered and muted as they were on the 4. Kim Deal’s singing on “Gigantic” by The Pixies is clean and easy to hear amidst the distorted guitars that wash over the chorus, and throughout Surfer Rosa, the separation of instruments and voices across the soundstage impressed me. The AirPods 5 sound better than other open-ear earbuds I’ve heard.

With iOS 27, Apple has added a 3-band EQ for those that want to tweak the sound. It’s not exclusive to these buds and will work with AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods Max 2 as well. The different bands don’t majorly change the sound profile, but it’s nice that Apple has finally included something for those who want to play around with it.

Call quality is also better than on the AirPods 4. While my voice sounded a bit compressed to those I talked to, they didn’t have any difficulty understanding me, and traffic sounds were imperceptible. The occasional conversation from someone passing by or strong breeze would sneak through the attenuation, but it was never too distracting.

The AirPods rest in the ear, but don’t go into the ear canal, which many find more comfortable and allows for better ambient awareness.

The AirPods 5 are the first non-Pro Apple earbuds to have swipe volume control on the stem.

The biggest disappointment with the AirPods 5 is their battery life. The buds are small, but only five hours with ANC on is below average and doesn’t even cover a cross-country flight. Battery life with the case has also decreased from 30 hours to 22. And for the base model AirPods 5, it’s even less — up to four hours on the earbuds, or up to 20 with the case. Putting the buds in their case for five minutes charges them up for another hour of listening.

If all you’re looking for is solid earbuds, there are lots of cheaper options that offer many of the same features. Earbuds like the Soundcore Liberty 4 NC and the Nothing Ear 3A are around $100 and have better noise canceling with sound quality that’s nearly as good. But neither of those have the same seamless integration with Apple products that the AirPods 5 do. And crucially, both of those are sealed earbuds, while the AirPods aren’t put into your ear canal at all, which some find more comfortable.

Apple’s open-ear earbuds design has never been my favorite. Silicone tips are more secure and provide superior active noise cancellation (although they come with their own fit challenges). But the AirPods 4 redesign, which felt more comfortable in my ears, started to sway me. Now with ANC at a cheaper price that includes volume control and a wireless charging case, the $149 AirPods 5 are great for someone who doesn’t like the feel of a sealed fit. I wouldn’t even bother with the less expensive AirPods 5.

Photography by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

title: GM updates its trucks’ native software to coexist with CarPlay
snippet: General Motors is polishing up the software experience in its bestselling trucks in an effort to reduce the amount of dangerous tapping and swiping that's required to access the most-used controls. It's also giving Apple CarPlay and Android Auto spiffy new picture-in-picture displays - which is notable given GM's previously stated hostility to phone mirroring in its electric vehicles. When the next-generation interface makes its debut on the 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 and 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 later this year, vehicle owners will see a number of changes, including slick new graphics for its advanced driver-assist system, animated transiti … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
General Motors is polishing up the software experience in its bestselling trucks in an effort to reduce the amount of dangerous tapping and swiping that’s required to access the most-used controls. It’s also giving Apple CarPlay and Android Auto spiffy new picture-in-picture displays — which is notable given GM’s previously stated hostility to phone mirroring in its electric vehicles.

When the next-generation interface makes its debut on the 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 and 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 later this year, vehicle owners will see a number of changes, including slick new graphics for its advanced driver-assist system, animated transitions between displays, and simplified layouts for heavy-duty truck stuff like trailering and off-roading. And they’ll be seeing it all on 60-plus inches of screen real estate — the combined size of instrument cluster, central display, and passenger screen in some of its trucks — that’s designed to enhance but not overwhelm the driving experience.

For GM, larger displays do not necessarily mean more distractions. Instead, the automaker views the additional space as an opportunity to be smarter about how information is presented and to make interactive elements larger, said Colin McCormick, group product manager for Google built-in, projection, and profiles at GM. Larger buttons and bigger tap zones can make the system easier to operate, particularly under difficult driving conditions, he said.

“The buttons can be larger and make it easier to do,” McCormick said. “Living in Michigan, the roads are terrible, so I’m trying to tap on a very small tap zone while hitting a bunch of potholes. These larger displays give you better functionality in that standpoint.”

1/4

There are still plenty of physical buttons for key functions like HVAC. But when you want to control the direction of the airflow, a new menu appears as a flyout. Customers have repeatedly professed their love for physical controls, so GM understands that moving key functions onto the screen just because there’s more real estate doesn’t necessarily earn them any goodwill. There are some formerly tangible tools that are now becoming digital only. The oil dipstick, for example, is now a virtual measurement that exists on the truck’s status screen. But the majority of the physical touchpoints remain physical.

Borrowing from the world of smartphone design, GM’s designers added a swipe-down notification interface for quick access to functions such as switching connected devices, entering settings, and privacy controls. Truck owners can disable the vehicle’s microphone directly from this interface, for example. The new interface also distinguishes between settings, which vehicle owners will likely visit once and then rarely ever again, and controls, which they may want to tweak more frequently.

GM wanted to address the complaint that its existing interface can feel disjointed because various functions abruptly take over the entire display, McCormick said. So rather than constantly replacing the entire screen, displays such as the media player can remain visible while an additional queue panel slides in from the side. By using animated transitions, the automaker is hoping to create a more contextual experience when moving between functions.

Lots of truck owners love to haul trailers, so GM put a particular focus on that experience with its new software designs. Trailering information now appears both in the driver information display and in the smaller homescreen card. The trucks include built-in trailer-aware navigation, so once a trailer is connected, the vehicle identifies it, and Google Maps can provide a route that accommodates the trailer. Customers enter the trailer’s dimensions, and those measurements can be carried from one vehicle to another through the customer’s GM account.

1/2GM is using picture-in-picture for Apple CarPlay…

But it’s when using Apple CarPlay or Android Auto that Chevy and GMC truck owners may see the most noticeable differences. Again, engineers were hoping to use the added screen real estate “intelligently,” McCormick said. And they didn’t want phone projection to completely take over the truck’s native infotainment, nor did they want to force customers to choose between them.

The solution: picture-in-picture phone mirroring, in which CarPlay and Android Auto occupy a large contextual card rather than taking over the entire screen. When a phone is connected through CarPlay, the phone icon changes into a CarPlay icon; selecting it brings up CarPlay within that large card. Pressing the native home button returns the driver to the split-screen home view. This allows customers to use Apple’s apps while retaining access to native GM functions, like trailering info.

The new layout is even more interesting when you consider GM’s seismic decision in 2023 to drop Apple CarPlay and Android from its EVs. Despite pushback from customers, GM has stood by its decision, arguing that it can deliver a better software experience to its customers without phone mirroring. GM CEO Mary Barra even suggested (in an interview on Decoder) the ban would eventually extend to the automaker’s gas-powered trucks and SUVs — only to walk it back days later.

That’s left GM to tweak CarPlay and Android Auto’s appearance in its Chevy and GMC trucks to enable the native GM-branded software experience to peek through. Phone projection will no longer occupy the entire screen, which McCormick argues was forcing drivers to switch back and forth when they needed to access their truck’s native controls. In this way, truck owners can choose to project their phone while also accessing key information, like trailering or off-roading details, McCormick said.

“I think we’re landing in a spot where… we don’t have a customer that has to decide, ‘Oh, I’m going to use projection, or, oh, I want to use the native system,’” he said. “That’s our sweet spot.”

The new UI will roll out to new Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks later this year, but only to new customers. Existing owners will be stuck with the previous-generation experience. The goal was to put the new interface on GM’s “bread-and-butter” trucks rather than first introducing it on lower-volume vehicles, which is more typical for a new experience, McCormick said. GM is so confident in the system that it’s launching it on its bestselling trucks so it can get in front of as many customers as possible.

GM sells close to 900,000 of these trucks a year, meaning the company expects to receive a substantial amount of feedback once the new interface is live and being used by customers. Some aspects of the first version may work extremely well, while others may need to be changed.

”We’ll take that experience, and the OTAs will allow us to get there,” McCormick said.

title: Spotify’s newest feature has been on my Apple Music wishlist for years
snippet: Today Spotify announced a feature every parent has probably asked for: the ability to exclude kids and family music from their algorithm. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Today Spotify announced a feature every parent has probably asked for: the ability to exclude kids and family music from their algorithm. Here are the details.

Parents can use new toggle so Spotify Wrapped and recommendations don’t include children’s music

A core feature of modern music streaming services is their ability to recommend music you’ll love.

But if you’re a parent, you know that children’s music has long been a blind spot for Spotify and Apple Music.

I have a toddler, so much of my Apple Music activity these days consists of Mickey Mouse Clubhouse and other children’s songs. Thus, my recommendations and Apple Music Replay are more tailored to my child than me.

But Spotify just launched the solution, and I really hope Apple follows suit soon. Per Spotify:

Starting today, we’re rolling out a new toggle in your settings that lets you exclude kids and family music from your taste profile, so those streams no longer shape your recommendations. This includes, for example, the songs you play on repeat from your kids’ favorite animated movies, theme songs from family TV shows, nursery rhymes, and more.

When you turn this setting off, you can still search for, listen to, and build playlists of kids and family music, but those streams won’t affect what Spotify suggests for you. That means experiences like Discover Weekly, Daily Mix, and Wrapped more accurately reflect your taste. And yes, it applies retroactively, so kids music you’ve already listened to won’t count toward your Wrapped top song or artist, for example.

I’m shocked at how long it took for a feature like this to arrive. But I’m thrilled that it’s finally here.

To use the new toggle, go to ‘Settings and privacy’ in the Spotify app, then ‘Content and display,’ and switch off the toggle labeled ‘Include kids and family music in taste profile.’

If you’re an Apple Music user, one alternative workaround is to use Focus modes to toggle listening history on and off. But I imagine most parents won’t have the mental bandwidth to remember to switch modes back and forth constantly, so it’s not a great solution.

How do you handle streaming children’s music as a parent? Let us know in the comments.

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang tells Trump ‘we’re not going to let [an AI slowdown] happen’
snippet: Though Elon Musk and Sam Altman have supported Dario Amodei's calls to slow the pace of AI development, Jensen Huang seems to feel differently.
fullText:
While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was onstage at the All-In Summit on Monday morning in Los Angeles, he got a phone call that he couldn’t send to voicemail — it was from President Donald Trump.

“I’m onstage with the besties,” Huang told Trump, referring to the venture capitalists who host the podcast All-In, including tech investors Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, and White House advisers David Friedberg and David Sacks.

In a move that will spark night terrors for public relations professionals everywhere, Huang flaunted his comfort with the president by putting Trump on speaker for conference attendees to hear.

“The great thing about life is Jensen can develop the most complex computer chip in the world … but he can’t figure out how to put you on speaker,” Trump said on the phone. (Huang is likely aware of how speakerphones work; he was asking stagehands for an extra microphone so that he could project the call to the audience.)

Onstage, Huang and the All-In hosts had been discussing Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call to “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI.” SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have publicly said they agree with Amodei, while Huang’s views have diverged.

“They’re just playing right in the hands of a lot of people that don’t want to see it happen,” Trump said. “That could be political people. It could also be China. And we’re not going to let that happen. It’s a hoax.”

“You’re right. We’re not going to let that happen, sir,” Huang replied as the crowd broke into applause.

Trump and his allies, like Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, have stated their belief that the growing sentiment against data center construction is part of an international psyop to stifle American economic growth. But the source of the public’s concern is more straightforward. Recent Gallup polling shows that seven in 10 Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their area, with more than 50% of respondents citing the effect of data centers on environmental resources. About 20% said they were concerned about cost-of-living increases and effects on their quality of life.

“We have to be a little bit careful … We have to do things and we have to do them prudently, but that doesn’t mean we’re going to stop an industry,” Trump said to Huang. “So I’m with you all the way. I didn’t even know how you felt about it. I just hoped you felt the same way as me. We’re going to lead.”

She has also written for publications like Polygon, MTV, the Kenyon Review, NPR, and Business Insider. title: Fashion app Daydream uses Apple Intelligence to help you shop the outfits in your camera roll
snippet: Thanks to the launch of iOS 27, Daydream's app now includes features that can turn saved outfit photos into shoppable results and search for products through Siri without opening the app.
fullText:
Daydream, an AI-powered fashion discovery app, launched two new features on Monday to let iPhone users turn saved outfit photos into shoppable results and search for clothing and accessories through Siri, without opening the app.

The new features were built using Apple’s iOS 27 developer tools, which officially rolled out today. To use either feature, you’ll need an iPhone running iOS 27 with Siri AI enabled, along with the Daydream app installed. The app is free to download on iOS devices.

The first feature uses Apple’s image-context capabilities, letting users shop from images already saved in their Photos app. Daydream analyzes the outfit in the image, identifies its individual pieces, and automatically surfaces shoppable matches and similar styles from Daydream’s catalog of roughly 3 million products.

Image Credits:Daydream

That means a screenshot of an outfit found on Instagram or Pinterest could become the starting point for a shopping search. Daydream can break down the image into relevant items, such as a sweater, pants, shoes, or accessories, and match them with products available through its collection. If the exact item in the photo is still available, Daydream can match the image back to the retailer selling it. If it’s no longer available, the app will instead surface similar options.

It can also handle requests for variations on what appears in an image. “I like this sweater but want it in red,” for example, is the kind of request Daydream can understand, Julie Bornstein, co-founder and CEO of Daydream, explained to TechCrunch.

The second feature is a Siri-powered natural-language search function. Users can make requests by voice or text through Siri without having to open Daydream’s app.

A user could say, “Hey, Siri, search Daydream for a cool blazer for my board meeting on Monday,” and Daydream then provides results personalized to them.

Bornstein adds that the experience can be more tailored if users have set up Daydream’s “Style Passport,” which asks for details such as their sizes, preferred brands, personal style, and budget.

Image Credits:Daydream

The company joins a growing number of AI shopping tools designed to rethink product discovery, such as big names like Google and Amazon, as well as some smaller players like Onton and Alta. But Bornstein believes that Daydream’s latest features offer something special that a lot of these other tools just can’t match.

“Most visual search tools don’t have the fashion category expertise, so they return results that don’t feel accurate, from brands that aren’t credible, or they link you to nonshoppable images,” she said. 

The launch fits into Daydream’s broader bet on AI-powered fashion shopping. The company sees these new features as more than stand-alone shopping tools. Its longer-term ambition is to build a shopping agent.

“This is one step toward the bigger vision, [which is] a shopping agent that understands someone’s style well enough to work across every surface in their life, not just on one surface,” Bornstein said. “Expect us to keep going deeper into on-device intelligence and further into the everyday moments where people are already discovering things they want.”

Daydream’s app launched last year and touts that it has more than 1.5 million shoppers browsing products from more than 325 retailers and 10,000 brands. Its retail lineup includes brands such as Anthropologie, Dolce & Gabbana, Uniqlo, J.Crew, Reformation, Gucci, and Nordstrom.

title: Waymo opens robotaxi service in Las Vegas
snippet: Las Vegas will be Waymo's 15th commercial robotaxi market.
fullText:
Waymo has begun to open up its robotaxi service to the public in Las Vegas, just a few weeks after receiving final approval from Nevada transportation regulators.

The Alphabet-owned company said Monday it will invite public riders on a rolling basis, following a robotaxi launch playbook it has followed in 14 other cities. 

Waymo is starting with “dozens” of its new Ojai minivan robotaxis, which will serve an area of Las Vegas that includes the Strip south of Highway 589 and into Boulder Junction, according to a spokesperson. Waymo’s fleet and service area will eventually scale. For now, members of the public will have to request an invite and hope to receive an access code. Typically, Waymo opens the service up to everyone within a month or two of its official launch.

The announcement follows a busy few weeks for Waymo as it tries to ramp up its operations across the United States and Europe as Tesla, Zoox, and other competitors attempt to close on its lead. Earlier this month, the company began offering its robotaxis to invited members of the public in Denver, San Diego, and Tampa.

Image Credits:Waymo

Las Vegas, where competitors Tesla and Motional are also planning to launch commercial robotaxi services, is Waymo’s 15th market. Zoox is already operating a commercial service in Las Vegas. Waymo also operates in Austin, Dallas, Houston, Los Angeles, Miami, Nashville, Phoenix, and the San Francisco Bay Area. The company launched, and then paused, service in San Antonio.

Waymo’s entry into Las Vegas follows approval by the Nevada Transportation Authority to operate commercial robotaxi services in Clark County, home to Las Vegas. Tesla and Uber also received approval from the agency.

Waymo has been authorized to operate up to 1,000 autonomous vehicles over the next year, Tesla is allowed to deploy up to 5,000, and Uber is allowed up to 1,000 robotaxis, which it will operate through partnerships with Hyundai subsidiary Motional and Zoox. Together, these permits would deploy up to 7,000 robotaxis across the county over the next 12 months.

It’s unlikely that the three companies will reach those numbers. Today, Waymo has a fleet of more than 4,000 robotaxis, which are spread across more than a dozen cities. During a meeting in August, Tesla’s Cybercab chief engineer Eric Early told state regulators that the company would be “extremely happy and satisfied if we could get ourselves up to 2,500, maybe a bit higher than that in the next year.”

Even without reaching those figures, the city could be saturated with robotaxis in the next year. 

Update: This article was updated to clarify that Zoox is already operating a commercial robotaxi service in Las Vegas.
