title: Let It Go: Here’s How to Keep Kids’ Music Out of Your Spotify Wrapped
snippet: You can still use your Spotify account to play Disney songs, but they won’t influence your recommendations or Wrapped roundup.
fullText:
For the first time in forever, your year-end Spotify Wrapped compilation can now reflect your own musical tastes, not your kids’ most-played songs.

Many Spotify users look forward to their Wrapped roundup, which comes out in early December. But if your Spotify account entertains a family throughout the year, your Wrapped may lean heavily on Disney tunes and Baby Shark. Now, you can fix that, doo-doo, doo-doo, doo-doo.

Kids’ and family music have been included in your Spotify taste profile by default. As of Tuesday, however, a new setting is rolling out globally on mobile for Free and Premium users, allowing you to opt out. If you choose this option, songs from kids’ animated movies, theme songs from family TV shows, nursery rhymes and similar tunes won’t influence your Spotify recommendations or listening insights, such as Wrapped.

If you choose to exclude family and kids’ music, you can still search for those tunes, listen to them and add them to playlists as much as you like. But that music will no longer appear in the personalized lists shaped by your top tracks — including Wrapped, Discover Weekly (a personalized playlist suggesting 30 songs every Monday) and Daily Mix (personalized playlists based on artists, moods and genres you play regularly).

To exclude kids’ and family music from your taste profile, tap your profile picture in the top-left corner of your Spotify account, go to Settings, select Content and Display and switch off the toggle that asks whether you want to include kids’ and family music in your taste profile. Spotify says it may take up to 48 hours for these changes to be reflected in your personalized recommendations. Then, it’ll be a whole new world for your Wrapped summary.

Better yet, it applies retroactively. So that day-long Frozen marathon you played back in the summer won’t show up in your Wrapped during the holidays.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Gael Cooper

She's been a journalist since 1989, working at Mpls.St.Paul Magazine, Twin Cities Sidewalk, the Minneapolis Star Tribune, and NBC News Digital. She's Gen X in birthdate, word and deed. title: Google upgrades all Gemini side panels in Workspace to have the same features
snippet: Gemini in Google Workspace can now “complete complex, cross-app tasks” from whatever app you’re working in. more…
fullText:
Gemini in Google Workspace can now “complete complex, cross-app tasks” from whatever app you’re working in.

Previously, the Gemini side panels found in each Workspace app had capabilities specific to that service: “generating a personalized document with Gemini required being in Docs while building AI-powered spreadsheets required being in Sheets.”

Google is now upgrading each instance of Gemini in Workspace to have the same feature set. This applies to the side panels in Gmail, Drive, Docs, Slides, and Chat. The upgrade is made possible by Workspace Intelligence and deeper app integrations.

For example, you can have Gemini “send an email to my sales team for their review and feedback” from Google Docs instead of needing to be in Gmail. 

	

In Google Chat, you can “find open times, schedule meetings, or resolve calendar conflicts.” Google Tasks also lets you “instantly log a reminder or create a to-do list” from any service.

On the content creation front, example prompts include:

When in Gmail (via the side panel) to create a doc: “Create a strategy brief for this project with goals, milestones and next steps.“

When in Gmail (via the side panel) to create a spreadsheet: “Create a tracker for this project in a new spreadsheet”

When in Docs (via the side panel) to create a deck: “Turn this proposal into an easy to read slide deck for my director using @presentation as a style reference.”

When in Chat (via Ask Gemini in Chat) to create a document: “Create a deck outlining Project Zebra with the latest updates”

When in Drive (via Ask Gemini in Drive) to create a document: “Create a customer insights deck from project Zebra using my project files including sheets, reports, and emails”

This expanded feature set started rolling out this month. For consumers, this is available to subscribers of Google AI Pro (“with the exception of scheduling functionality”) and Google AI Ultra. It’s also coming to:

Business: Standard and Plus

Enterprise: Standard and Plus

Other Editions: Frontline Plus (only for scheduling functionality)

Education Add-ons: Google AI Pro for Education

Other Add-ons: AI Expanded Access

title: Possible Google device at FCC could be Wear OS-powered fitness tracker
snippet: A new piece of hardware passed through FCC certification today, and the evidence points to it being a Wear OS-powered device made by Google. more…
fullText:
A new piece of hardware passed through FCC certification today, and the evidence points to it being a Wear OS-powered device made by Google.

This “Wireless Device” — as it’s officially labeled — comes from Goertek, which is already known for manufacturing various generations of Pixel Buds.

The “G8BL6” model name matches Google’s usual pattern for first-party hardware. Meanwhile, the e-label points to the existence of a screen, with the access method being Settings > System > Regulatory Information. That is identical to how you access the e-label on the Pixel Watch today. 

This would suggest the presence of Wear OS, with that possibility further bolstered by how the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) was leveraged during the testing process.

	

On the connectivity front, this device has Bluetooth LE and Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), or GPS. The former uses a “Metal frame Antenna.”

Taken together, G8BL6 is most likely a Google fitness tracker powered by Wear OS, though the lack of Wi-Fi is curious. This would be a new form factor for the platform, raising questions about whether the OS is battery-efficient enough.

This filing comes as an unknown Google tracker was spotted in Pixel 11 advertising this August. We saw a vertical, pill-shaped display with a Pixel Watch-esque band. The watch face is very familiar, down to the existing Wear OS complications for fitness.

Following the Fitbit Air, this would make sense as a successor to the popular Fitbit Charge line, which is currently priced at $160 and last updated in 2023.

title: Apple’s iPhone Duo foldable has the same IP68 protection as Pixel Fold – temporary
snippet: Apple did the thing. The first foldable iPhone has arrived with the new iPhone Duo delivering a pretty compelling package for interested foldable customers who don’t want to give up on iOS. It also addresses a durability gap that few others have managed with IP68 protection but, like Pixel 11 Pro Fold, that’s only a temporary rating for the iPhone Duo. more…
fullText:
Apple did the thing. The first foldable iPhone has arrived with the new iPhone Duo delivering a pretty compelling package for interested foldable customers who don’t want to give up on iOS. It also addresses a durability gap that few others have managed with IP68 protection but, like Pixel 11 Pro Fold, that’s only a temporary rating for the iPhone Duo.

In a footnote on Apple’s iPhone Duo listing, the company admits that the IP68 dust/water protection won’t last forever:

iPhone Duo is splash, water, and dust resistant and was tested under controlled laboratory conditions with a rating of IP68 under IEC standard 60529 (maximum depth of 6 meters up to 30 minutes). Splash, water, and dust resistance are not permanent conditions. Resistance might decrease as a result of normal wear…

It’s a bit less of a thought for a typical slab-style smartphone, as the dust/water resistance there shouldn’t change drastically unless there is external damage. But, with a foldable, there are moving parts to account for and, as such, the rating may wane over time.

Apple’s not alone.

	

Google was the first to manage an IP68 rating on a foldable with last year’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold, a spec that’s since carried on to the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. In Google’s own footnote, the company explains:

Designed to comply with dust and water protection rating IP68 under IEC standard 60529 when each device leaves the factory but the device is not water or dust proof. The accessories are not water or dust resistant. Water resistance and dust resistance are not permanent conditions and will diminish or be lost over time due to normal wear and tear, device repair, disassembly or damage. Phone is not drop/tumble proof and dropping your device may result in loss of water/dust resistance.

As pointed out in our comments, Google also carries the same disclaimer on standard Pixel phones, but the same isn’t true of every brand. Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro listings, for example, don’t mention anything about the water resistance waning. Honor does say the same about its Magic V6 foldable, with the IP68/69 rating “not permanently effective, and the protective performance may decrease due to daily wear and tear,” with the same disclaimer on Magic 8 Pro. Foldables are still more prone to this problem than typical slab smartphones, though.

title: Why Is My iPhone ‘Optimizing Search and Siri’ With iOS 27?
snippet: This process could take a few hours or longer, but your iPhone will still work in that time.
fullText:
After you upgrade your iPhone to iOS 27, you might notice your device doing a little extra thinking. That’s because the update brings a revamped Search system to your device, and it needs some time to get to know everything on your iPhone. 

You can download iOS 27 now by going to Settings > General > Software Update > Update Now and following the prompts on your screen.

At June’s Worldwide Developers Conference, Apple announced that it was rebuilding its Search interface for iOS 27. The company said the restructure would make searching across your device faster, more reliable and more accurate. In order to do that, iOS 27 has to reindex items across your iPhone. So after you update, you’ll see a banner in Settings that reads “Optimizing Search and Siri.” This is a normal part of the update, and it could take a while to finish, but the good news is you can still use your iPhone during this process.

Here’s what you need to know about the indexing and optimization process once you download iOS 27.

What is indexing?

Data indexing is the process of scanning and organizing metadata from data assets into an index so it can be easily searched.

“Think of it like the index of a book,” data management company Komprise wrote online. “[The index] doesn’t hold the content, but it tells you where to find it, and what’s inside.”

Apple’s support page about Spotlight indexing says that Spotlight search indexes your iPhone when you first set up your device, as data changes on your device and after you update your iPhone. So your device has reindexed before and you likely never noticed – I know I didn’t.

Apple also notes that your iPhone’s index “stays on your device and isn’t shared with Apple or your other devices.” 

Indexing can take hours or days

You can still use your iPhone, even when it’s indexing.LuckyDuck via Getty Images

Apple’s support page notes that indexing could take anywhere from a couple hours to a few days. When I updated my iPhone to a beta version of iOS 27, my iPhone took a couple hours to index, but the more stuff you have stored on your phone, the longer it will take. 

The process takes longer this time around because Apple rebuilt its Search interface in iOS 27. So the update isn’t just adding a few more things to the index, it’s implementing a new search system. 

That means the system isn’t just crawling through the new stuff — it needs to go back through all the data in your phone. Think of it like cataloging new items you’ve bought versus creating an inventory of everything in your home.

Apple does offer a few suggestions on how to speed up the process:

Plug your device into a power source.

Connect your device to Wi-Fi.

Don’t use your iPhone.

OK, can I still use my iPhone?

You can! Indexing doesn’t prevent you from using your iPhone, but it goes faster if you set the phone aside.

If you do use your iPhone during the process, your Spotlight search results might be incomplete because it hasn’t finished indexing. Otherwise, your device should operate as usual. Which is good because I couldn’t imagine going without my phone for a few days at this point – don’t judge me. 

Spotlight search still not working? 

If your iPhone is finished indexing – the banner in Settings will go away – and you’re still running into issues, you should review your Search settings and make sure Spotlight has access to your apps. Here’s how to check. 

Tap Settings.

Tap Search.

From here, you can adjust what shows up in Spotlight, and near the bottom of the menu, you can review which apps Spotlight has access to. You can tap into each app to grant or revoke Spotlight permission. 

However, there doesn’t seem to be a way to grant or revoke Spotlight access across all apps at once, so you have to go into each individual app to do this. 

For more on Apple, here’s what to know about the iPhone Duo and everything Apple announced at its “Surprise and shine” event.

							Senior writer

title: The Google Pixel is fine and all, but still needs a ‘Ryzen moment’ [Video]
snippet: At what stage does “fine” feel like it’s doing heavy lifting for problems that might appear in the future? It’s something talked about around the Tensor chip in Pixel phones, but isn’t it about time we saw real-world performance gains? The truth is, we probably need a Ryzen moment for the Tensor chip. more…
fullText:
At what stage does “fine” feel like it’s doing heavy lifting for problems that might appear in the future? It’s something talked about around the Tensor chip in Pixel phones, but isn’t it about time we saw real-world performance gains? The truth is, we probably need a Ryzen moment for the Tensor chip.

For those who aren’t fully plugged into the history of desktop computing, AMD, or “Team Red,” long languished behind Intel when it came to desktop-tier performance CPUs. 

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

The Bulldozer architecture used on the FX series of chips was a bit of a disaster. Intel capitalized on this misstep completely, locking the consumer market into a complacent four-core monopoly for nearly a decade because it simply had no pressure to innovate.

	

With this percolating in the back of my mind, during a recent podcast episode, and spurred on by a Reddit comment I can no longer find over on /r/GooglePixel, there’s a strange sense of déjà vu applicable to Google’s smartphone lineup. There needs to be more than just incremental gains and AI being touted on a $1,000 phones best chip. 

Side note: if you are the original poster, please get in touch; you had me thinking about this more broadly and deserve credit for doing so.

While it’s hard not to laud the Pixel line for the brilliant software, extensive and unmatched feature drops, and mostly excellent camera processing, it’s the Google Tensor processor that is almost always the biggest caveat or talking point. 

Right now, the Tensor lineup has spent years echoing the systemic flaws of AMD’s Bulldozer era. Stumbling, faltering, and just about hanging in there. I think most of us can agree that Google doesn’t just need an incremental chip upgrade. To truly unlock the potential of the Pixel line, the company needs its very own “Ryzen moment.”

Back to Bulldozer for a second, because I’m not sure everyone is fully aware of chips built on this architecture. FX chips ran hot and throttled under load, were power-hungry, and, in many cases, lost to AMD’s own previous-generation Phenom II chips in terms of performance. They were able to cling to survival more because of very low prices than anything else.

Bulldozer was ditched in favor of the Zen project. Each successive architectural enhancement saw improvements, and in 2017, the first Ryzen 1000 series desktop processors blew everyone out of the water. Multi-threaded performance that rivaled $1,000+ chips from the market leader, Intel. Since then, AMD has been on a tear with Ryzen, beating a complacent Intel in practically all areas.

You can see the parallels between these mid-2010s AMD CPUs and the last few generations of Google’s Tensor chips, but this feels like the perfect blueprint.

It definitely feels that, like AMD in 2012, Google is sacrificing pure hardware efficiency in favor of trying to capture something less important, all while trying to lean into the key AI selling point. It’s a big, bold bet that makes less sense to true tech nerds, as most of the best off-the-shelf Qualcomm chips are, in many ways and metrics, better at AI processing right now than Tensor.

Some of the early Tensor problems fall at Samsung’s doorstep. Exynos chips have never had a great reputation, and relying on Samsung Foundry likely meant some limitations. You may also remember that Qualcomm briefly switched manufacturing to Samsung’s 4nm node for the Snapdragon 8 Gen 1. The chipmaker later moved production to TSMC for the follow-up Snapdragon 8+ Gen 1 chip due to poor manufacturing yields and efficiency issues with Samsung Foundry. This prompted substantial efficiency gains with heat reduction and sustained performance improvements.

Maybe Google eventually realized it needed a similar escape route and took similar steps. Alas, this hasn’t quite worked out to do what maybe we as nerds wanted. The pre-launch talk around the transition to TSMC manufacturing was probably spurred on more by hope than anything concrete – despite numerous leaks. 

I, like many others, expected a clean-slate architecture built on a superior node might finally deliver the performance gains that had been sorely missing for four generations. It’s frustrating and annoying that this hasn’t come to fruition.

Fast forward to the present day. We are now two generations into Google’s TSMC era, with the Tensor G5 and the current Tensor G6 powering the Pixel 11 lineup.

This transition has only eradicated some of the problems, but still leaves us with a now glaring performance gap. The year-over-year gains have been respectable increments, but they are not quite the massive generational “leaps” fans were hoping for before the switch.

I’m tempering my ire a little bit, though. We’ve not seen any major gains yet, but the groundwork is at the very least in place. That said, there’s only so long the company can allow Qualcomm to keep building an enormous performance gap.

A performance gap that, let’s be real, lots of people don’t care all that much about when using their phone. I’d put myself in that category, but I’d be lying if I said it wouldn’t be nice to have a Qualcomm-beating chip that can do everything a modern phone can without breaking a sweat.

While I might not be too disappointed, this matters to people buying phones, especially $1,000 phones. It helps market your product, selling on the promise of unrivaled performance. The Tensor platform is “fine” in that you likely won’t feel a major difference texting or looking at Instagram, and it’s true that Google tunes Android to feel as fluid as possible on a Pixel phone. Intensive things? It’s a bit of a mixed bag and a different story.

My question is, why make it harder for the engineers? A little extra breathing room would be more than welcome by practically everyone. By allowing Qualcomm and Apple to build an enormous, compounding performance gap year after year, Google is playing a dangerous game.

It limits what the phone can handle when pushed, whether that means recording extended 4K video clips without getting a thermal warning or processing heavy background tasks. That’s not to mention the things we’re missing out on, like local 8K video recording and many other video-centric functions that rival premium devices have shipped with for years.

More importantly, this performance gap directly threatens Google’s industry-leading promise of seven years of OS updates. 

I probably don’t need to tell you that a chip that feels just about “good enough” today will likely struggle under the weight of Android operating systems in the late 2020s and early 2030s. I’m still worried about the long-term longevity and thermal headroom required to ensure a Pixel actually lasts through its promised support window. 

7 years is a long time, and with prices ballooning and no sign of coming down any time soon, there are people who will be keeping their phones longer into that support lifecycle than ever before. Using a phone for 5 years without switching is likely to become the norm.

Apple is another parallel that Google has to keep in mind, and they show exactly where the broader computing landscape is going.

Look at what Cupertino did earlier this year with the MacBook Neo. They took the A18 Pro, which is a smartphone chip, and threw it straight into a fanless, entry-level laptop running a full, desktop-grade operating system. They didn’t need to strip macOS down or compromise the user experience to make it happen. The silicon is simply so efficient and so inherently powerful that it treats a desktop workflow like a walk in the park.

This laptop paradigm is precisely why Google desperately needs a high-performance breakthrough. It isn’t just about making the Pixel 11 feel snappy because there’s a bigger ecosystem picture that needs to be considered. The company has spent the last couple of years laying the foundation for full desktop windowing in Android. It’s clear that the company wants devices to function as actual desktop machines the second you hook them up to an external monitor.

Imagine a future first-party Googlebook, or a pro-tier Android productivity tablet that docks into a mouse and keyboard setup, running entirely off the custom silicon in your pocket. I’m still surprised it hasn’t taken off, given how futuristic it seems to my millennial brain, but if there is any life in this vision, it completely lives and dies by the quality of the processor. Which is likely why most people are happy to stick to a dedicated laptop plus mobile in most cases.

If Google wants Android to transition from a mobile OS into a genuine productivity system that spans phones, laptops, and potentially desktops, Tensor cannot just be an “okay” component for scrolling social media. It needs the raw architectural grunt to act as a proper desktop computer without turning into a pocket-warmer.

When AMD launched Ryzen in 2017, the initial 1000-series chips didn’t instantly obliterate Intel in pure single-core speed. It took time, patience, and consecutive generational refinements with Zen 2 and Zen 3 to achieve complete, undeniable dominance, especially in the gaming space.

Moving to TSMC hasn’t instantly gifted Google the mobile performance crown with the Tensor G5 or G6; it at least feels like the company has finally established a stable, thermally efficient base to iterate on. The iterating is definitely tiny right now, but I’m desperately hoping a breakthrough might come with the next version.

	

For years, Google’s Android engineers have been performing optimization miracles, almost shoehorning what I would consider the best mobile software to glide smoothly over what some might call “compromised” hardware.

What kind of funny is that despite this, Pixel phones do often age better as a result, but engineering shouldn’t be an endless exercise in potential damage control. Hand-waving the Pixel 11 performance as good enough sometimes feels reductive, and there’s only so many times it can be deemed acceptable. We need chipset performance gains, not just more AI papering over cracks. To weaken my argument somewhat, I don’t doubt they will come with more time.

If we get a true Ryzen moment with their custom TSMC architecture in the coming generations, Google can finally market the Pixel ecosystem on the promise of unrivaled, unthrottled performance across phones, tablets, and heck, maybe even desktops if Android works on the form factor. The foundation is poured, and the blueprints are drawn. It is time for Google to stop compromising and finally unleash its inner Team Red.

title: Here’s everything new for Apple Wallet in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 launched today for iPhone, here’s what’s new for the Apple Wallet app in the latest major software update. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 launched today for iPhone, here’s what’s new for the Apple Wallet app in the latest major software update.

Create a Pass

Apple Wallet is always improving, including several recent updates in iOS 26. But iOS 27 brings even more new features to Wallet users.

Create a Pass is a new feature you’ll find when you hit the + button inside iOS 27’s Wallet app.

It enables you to create a pass in one of two ways: 

Scan a physical pass to import it using your iPhone’s camera and visual intelligence

Create a pass manually from scratch

The former requires the next-gen Apple Intelligence capabilities. Creating a pass manually, meanwhile, provides you with three options: Standard, Membership, and Event.

The goal is that Apple wants to make the Wallet app your go-to hub for all kinds of passes, whether they’re digital or physical.

Split Bill with Apple Cash

Split Bill with Apple Cash is another iOS 27 addition to Wallet.

When using the new Siri mode in the Camera app to scan a receipt, you’ll see the option to Split Bill with Apple Cash.

From here, the Wallet app opens and you’ll be presented with options to ‘Request’ payment from others or ‘Pay Your Share.’ It’s quick, easy, and offers another reason to use Apple Cash.

Recurring transactions for Apple Card

If you use Apple Card, there’s a convenient new hub in iOS 27 for all your recurring transactions.

Behind the three-dot icon in the top-right corner of the Apple Card screen, there’s a new ‘Recurring’ option.

This shows you all upcoming recurring transactions. You can see them on a calendar month view, or listed out.

Essentially, this new section provides an easy way to track current subscriptions and anticipate upcoming charges.

Hotel Key upgrades

Beyond some small UI updates and a refreshed app icon, the last noteworthy iOS 27 feature for Apple Wallet involves hotel keys.

Per a press release, here’s what Apple says is coming to hotel keys soon:

With iOS 27, Apple Wallet will offer an enhanced key experience for participating hotels and resorts. Today’s key experience allows guests to seamlessly unlock their rooms and hotel amenities using their iPhone or Apple Watch. And with the new enhanced key experience, they will also be able to view even more details about their trips, receive timely updates about booked activities, access services available during their stay, and more — all in one place in Apple Wallet.

iOS 27 also adds an ‘Insights’ feature to Wallet for users in select territories. It lets you track spending across multiple cards. But in the US at least, that feature isn’t available despite being present in some iOS 27 betas.

title: Apple now accepting App Store submissions built for iOS 27, macOS 27, more
snippet: Developers can now submit apps built for iOS 27 and Apple’s other new operating system releases, ahead of their official rollout next Monday. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Developers can now submit apps built for iOS 27 and Apple’s other new operating system releases, ahead of their official rollout next Monday. Here are the details.

Developers can now submit iOS 27-ready apps

During yesterday’s “Surprise and Shine” event, Apple confirmed that iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, tvOS 27, visionOS 27, and watchOS 27 will launch next Monday, September 14.

Today, Apple announced that developers can now download the Xcode 27 Release Candidate and submit apps and games built with the latest SDKs for approval.

Apple also took the opportunity to remind developers that macOS 27 will only support software built for Apple silicon:

Optimize your app for macOS 27. macOS 26 is the final release supporting Intel Mac computers and Rosetta — macOS 27 will be Apple silicon only. To limit your app to Macs with Apple silicon, set your Xcode build architecture to arm64 only, then rebuild and resubmit. Removing support for Intel-based apps lets you further simplify your development and optimize your app for Apple silicon.

Additionally, Apple reminded developers to answer the new age rating questions required for features such as Time Allowances, and encouraged them to prepare their App Store listings for the new product page headers and search result assets, with updated design guidance and templates available for product pages, screenshots, app previews, and In-App Events.

Finally, Apple reaffirmed that “starting April 2027, apps and games uploaded to App Store Connect need to meet the following minimum requirements”:

iOS and iPadOS apps must be built with the iOS 27 & iPadOS 27 SDK or later

tvOS apps must be built with the tvOS 27 SDK or later

visionOS apps must be built with the visionOS 27 SDK or later

watchOS apps must be built with the watchOS 27 SDK or later

The more important feature is the fact that the prongs can adjust based on which position you want the display to be in. It also comes in 4 colors: blue, white, black, and orange. You can buy one on Amazon for $29.99.

This won’t charge your iPhone 18 Pro with the fastest speeds, though it will get quite close. For the highest speeds, you’ll need the next charger on the list.

Apple 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max

This oddly named power adapter from last year will support the highest speed fast charging on iPhone 18 Pro, according to Apple’s website. It’s exactly what you’d expect from an Apple charger, and it’s available on Amazon for $34.99.

With its up to 60W capacity thanks to Adjustable Voltage Supply, you can charge an iPhone 18 Pro up to 50% in just 15 minutes.

Anker Nano 70W

If you want a charger you can use for multiple things, the Anker Nano 70W is a fantastic choice. It’ll charge your iPhone 18 Pro to the fullest, whilst also being able to provide a sufficient charge for a base model 14” MacBook Pro or MacBook Air. It has three ports: two USB-C and one USB-A.

It also comes with a built in 5ft USB-C cable, and is priced at just $39.99 on Amazon.

ESR 3-in-1 CryoBoost MagSafe Stand

At $99.99 on Amazon, its one of the cheaper options that supports active cooling whilst also coming with a sufficient power adapter in the box.

title: Google rolls out Motion Assist bubbles to Pixel, Samsung
snippet: After announcing earlier this month, Google has rolled out Motion Assist to Pixel and Samsung phones running Android 17. more…
fullText:
After announcing earlier this month, Google has rolled out Motion Assist to Pixel and Samsung phones running Android 17.

The aim is to reduce motion sickness when you’re in a car, bus, or other moving vehicle with an onscreen bubbles overlay that adjusts to the device’s motion.

To enable, search for “motion assist” in the Settings app or open the Quick Settings editor and scroll down to “From system apps” (on Pixel). The long route is Settings app > Google > All services tab > Personal & device safety > Motion assist. Part of Google Play services, it appears alongside Advanced Protection and Theft protection.

This menu lets you have Motion Assist automatically “Start in a moving vehicle,” but Google also recommends adding a Quick Settings Tile to manually enable and disable “from any screen.” Once active, there’s also a silent system notification that lets you disable with a tap. On most phones, you get two columns of shapes on the left and right edges.

	

The Customize menu lets you adjust:

Color: Based on system (Dynamic Color), Red, Yellow, Green, Blue

Shape: Circle, Square, Pentagon, Diamond

Opacity: Slider

Randomization: “Color and shape change every few seconds”

As of today, Motion Assist has widely rolled out on all our Google Pixel and Samsung Galaxy (Fold 8 series) devices running Android 17. Be sure to restart your phone if it’s not yet live. We’re seeing the bubbles with version 26.33.32 of Google Play services.

title: Battery draining faster after updating to iOS 27? Don’t panic …
snippet: If you’ve just updated your iPhone to iOS 27, you may have felt concerned after seeing your battery draining faster than usual, as well as your device getting hot in normal use. If so, there’s no cause for panic. While both effects may be very real, they are only temporary … more…
fullText:
If you’ve just updated your iPhone to iOS 27, you may have felt concerned after seeing your battery draining faster than usual, as well as your device getting hot in normal use.

If so, there’s no cause for panic. While both effects may be very real, they are only temporary … 

Any time you update to a new version of iOS, there will be some things going on in the background for some time afterwards. This is particularly true for major updates.

These CPU-intensive background processes will often see your iPhone getting hotter than usual, and consuming significantly more battery power. Apple specifically warns about this.

Immediately after completing an update, particularly a major release, you might notice a temporary impact on battery life and thermal performance. This is normal, because your device needs time to complete the setup process in the background, including indexing data and files for search, downloading new assets, and updating apps.

The impact of iOS 27 is bigger than usual, thanks to the need to completely re-index your device for use with Siri AI. This process may last several days.

The good news is that once all of the background processing has completed, your device will return to normal. Indeed, the efficiency of iOS 27 means that you may find that battery life is improved once the update has finished all of the under-the-hood work.

snippet: A new iPhone announcement always means a mad rush for accessories that will arrive when your new device arrives, and this year that includes an entirely new category with the iPhone Duo. ESR is a well-respected name in Apple accessories, and its iPhone 18 lineup covers the new iPhone Duo, the iPhone 18 Pro models, and everything that goes with them: charging, AirPods, Apple Watch, and MagSafe wallets. fullText:
A new iPhone announcement always means a mad rush for accessories that will arrive when your new device arrives, and this year that includes an entirely new category with the iPhone Duo. ESR is a well-respected name in Apple accessories, and its iPhone 18 lineup covers the new iPhone Duo, the iPhone 18 Pro models, and everything that goes with them: charging, AirPods, Apple Watch, and MagSafe wallets. Here’s a look at what’s coming from ESR for Apple’s new iPhone lineup.

Atelier Vegan Leather Case for the iPhone Duo

The headliner of the new iPhone lineup is the ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand for the iPhone Duo. As we’ve seen with Android phones, cases for folding phones can be a hard design problem to solve. You’re aiming to protect the two halves of a phone, the hinge, and the exterior screen, all without adding a massive amount of bulk. People bought an iPhone Duo specifically because it folds thin, so ESR built a premium case truly suited for modern everyday carry.

The team started with how it looks and feels, because that’s what you notice first. The Atelier material is made from high-quality organic silicone leather with a delicate, soft touch and a skin-friendly texture. It’s the kind of premium look that stays refined through everyday use rather than looking worn after a month in a pocket. Said another one: It’ll age like fine wine. ESR also added an anti-fouling coating and treated the light-colored TPU surface with a stain-resistant finish, so it resists stains from daily use and cleans up easily. ESR’s tagline for this case is “For the Look That Lasts,” and the combination of a high-end feel with long-term durability is exactly what that’s getting at.

The Flex Stand is another incredible reason to make this your everyday iPhone Duo case. It’s a 180-degree rotating stand built from high-strength zinc alloy, with a precision hinge and optimized damping force control that delivers a smooth, fluid opening and closing experience. An internal damping-locking design keeps it stable at multiple angles, folded or unfolded, and the zinc alloy construction prevents deformation even after prolonged use, propping up your iPhone Duo. ESR has tested it through 3,000 open and close cycles. Open to view, close to protect. It’s really that simple.

The protection and magnetic hold round out what is a compelling case for your iPhone Duo.  You get extra hinge protection, a soft microfiber lining with a TPU frame, and raised-edge protection. If you follow our MagSafe Monday column, you know that ESR brings the power (literally) when it comes to MagSafe: 1,400g of magnetic strength from a built-in high-strength magnet, so wireless chargers, car mounts, card holders, and power banks all snap on and hold strong.

The same case for iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max

The Atelier case also comes in iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max versions and carries the same premium materials as the iPhone Duo version. The back is high-quality organic silicone leather with a delicate, soft touch and a skin-friendly surface texture, so it stays refined through everyday use. ESR added the same anti-fouling coating and stain-resistant treatment to the light-colored TPU surface, so daily debris and stains wipe away instead of setting in and showing wear and tear. Spill coffee on it? It’ll clean it up effortlessly. That’s the whole idea behind ESR’s “For the Look That Lasts” belief. 

The Flex Stand on the iPhone 18 and 18 Pro edition adjusts from 15 to 69 degrees for portrait and landscape viewing, covering StandBy on your nightstand and video on a plane ride. It has the same dual-function design as the iPhone Duo version: open to view, close to protect, with no separate stand to carry.

On protection, the Pro version steps things up. It offers 3x military-grade protection, including 12-foot drop protection, plus a built-in Camera Control cover, a soft microfiber lining with a TPU frame that guards the edges against scratches, and raised-edge protection. It has the same 1,400g magnetic hold, with a precise magnetic ring layout that lets MagSafe accessories align quickly and automatically. That means stable compatibility with wireless chargers, car mounts, card holders, and power banks, all in a versatile, everyday-carry-ready design.

UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector

For ultimate protection, ESR’s UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector covers both the iPhone Duo and the full iPhone 18 Pro lineup. Armorite Pro is ESR’s toughened screen protector line, made with Accessory Glass by Corning™, the same company that has made the durable glass in Apple products since the very first iPhone.

In non-tech speak: this is real and hardened glass rather than generic tempered glass, which ESR’s lab testing puts at 10x the impact absorption of generic protectors you find all over the internet and in retail stores.

Accessory Glass by Corning™ also offers up to 2x better scratch resistance per Corning’s lab testing, and it features an anti-reflective coating that reduces light reflection to just 2.3% while maintaining 94% optical transmittance. This gives you less glare and truer color, so you’re not trading screen quality for additional protection.

Then there’s installation, which is where it can go wrong, and customers end up frustrated. You shouldn’t need professional installation for a screen protector. Everyone has been through this process: you line it up, press it down, and there’s a single stray piece of lint under the glass that you’ll stare at for the next year. ESR’s UltraFit tray is built to prevent exactly this annoyance. It’s a one-pull system that takes two steps. You set the tray over your phone, pull the tab, and the tray’s design lifts dust off the screen and pushes air bubbles out as the protector goes down. On a brand-new iPhone Duo or iPhone 18 Pro, getting this right the first time matters, and the tray does the heavy lifting for you.

Cyclone 25W Magnetic Charging Pad with CryoBoost

On the MagSafe charging side, the Cyclone 25W Magnetic Charging Pad with CryoBoost keeps your iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo charged while staying cool. Qi2 25W is the newer wireless charging standard that pushes magnetic charging speeds up to 25W, well past the 7.5W MagSafe accessories that were stuck at for years with the old standard, so wireless finally stops feeling like the slow option.

CryoBoost is ESR’s patented active cooling technology: a built-in fan that reduces phone heat during charging while remaining under 25 dB. The 9to5Mac team has had this device for a few weeks and can verify it is virtually silent. Cooling matters for more than just charging speed. Heat wears down a lithium-ion battery over time, so a charger that actively dissipates heat protects your iPhone’s long-term battery health, not just topping it off faster today. That’s the kind of benefit you notice two years in rather than two minutes in. 

It also includes an adjustable stand that rotates from 0 to 150 degrees, which makes it really functional and useful around the house and at the office. You can prop it up in the kitchen to follow a recipe while your phone charges, angle it for StandBy mode on your nightstand as you go to bed, or turn it landscape for a movie. On a desk, it doubles as a stand that keeps your iPhone visible for notifications and FaceTime while it charges. It’s one device that works for the kitchen, the nightstand, and the desk instead of needing a different charger in every room. Discount code: MB078982.

Rounding out the charging lineup is the ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger, a compact wall charger with a built-in retractable braided cable that extends to just over 3 feet, giving you enough reach to charge comfortably without being tethered right beside an outlet. The braided cable is rated for 20,000 pulls and retractions and 10,000 bends, so it’s built to survive daily use rather than fray after a few months in your bag. It’s powered by the PD 3.2 AVS protocol, which means it delivers up to 60W dynamic power, enough to fast charge your MacBook Air. ESR’s own testing shows it can charge an iPhone 18 Pro to 50% in 15 minutes. On top of all of this, it has a second USB-C port so it can handle everything you need at home, at the office, or on the go. Discount code: MJARV5BO.

ESR also released the new Xtend 100W Retractable Car Charger, which charges your laptop and a phone simultaneously via separate 67W and 33W outputs. ESR’s internal testing shows that the C1 cable delivers up to 67W of power, charging an iPhone 18 Pro to 50% in just 15 minutes or a MacBook Pro to 65% in 35 minutes. Both cables are built into the charger and fully retract when you’re done, so there are no loose cables in the car when they aren’t in use. A third USB-C port handles a second phone, headphones, a portable game system, etc. The built-in USB-C cables extend to just over 3 feet, include built-in over-voltage/under-voltage protection and real-time temperature monitoring, and keep charging up to 15°C cooler than your standard car chargers. Discount code: ESR2B531.

AirPods, Apple Watch, and your wallet

Have you ever dropped your AirPods and had your earbuds go flying? Never again with the ESR Cyber FlickLock Magnetic Case. FlickLock is a patented slide mechanism that swaps the internal magnets between attracting and repelling, so the lid locks shut with maximum magnetic force for drop protection, but pops open with a one-handed flick. It’s the perfect everyday-carry AirPods case. It’s tested through 20,000 uses, works great with MagSafe charging, and comes in options for AirPods Pro 3, Pro 2/1, and AirPods 5/4.

The ESR Equinox Watch Band pairs a secure pin-and-fold lock with skin-friendly, ventilated material and a look that goes from a morning workout to a board meeting. It works with Apple Watch Ultra 1-4, Series 1-12. Finally, the ESR Armorite® Pro Protection Set for the Apple Watch Ultra (1-4) uses Accessory Glass by Corning™ for up to 2x better scratch resistance and up to 25% less scratch visibility, and both the protector and case go on fast, no strap removal required.

Rounding out the accessory ecosystem for your new iPhone, the ESR Geo Magnetic Wallet Stand is the first MagSafe wallet with full Apple-certified Find My support, now with Siri voice search, so you can ask Siri to find your wallet when you inevitably set it down somewhere. It holds 5 cards with a clear driver’s license window, includes RFID blocking and a finger-loop grip, and doubles as a multi-view iPhone stand. If you are looking for an everyday carry MagSafe wallet for your new iPhone, look no further than this innovative option.

Wrap up

Apple has ushered in a new era with the iPhone Duo while delivering an incredible iPhone 18 lineup. New iPhone releases are only half the story every fall. The accessories determine how you actually live with the device on a daily basis, and the iPhone Duo raises the stakes on getting that right. It’s more than just getting the right case. ESR’s accessory ecosystem charges your iPhone and AirPods at home and on the go while protecting your entire lineup from day-to-day wear and tear.

ESR built its new iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 lineup around that need: trustworthy protection, faster and cooler charging, and everyday-carry gear that does more than one job. The new iPhones are here, and ESR is ready to complete your experience. Follow ESR on X and Facebook to keep up to date on all their latest releases.

title: iPhone Duo is thicker and heavier than basically every Android foldable
snippet: The days of foldables being an Android-only experience are over. The iPhone Duo is set to arrive next month for a relatively-competitive $2,000 price point, and it seems like Apple’s decision to sit back and observe since the launch of the original Galaxy Fold more or less paid off — that is, until you consider the iPhone Duo’s size and shape. more…
fullText:
The days of foldables being an Android-only experience are over. The iPhone Duo is set to arrive next month for a relatively-competitive $2,000 price point, and it seems like Apple’s decision to sit back and observe since the launch of the original Galaxy Fold more or less paid off — that is, until you consider the iPhone Duo’s size and shape.

I won’t lie — there’s plenty of things I find intriguing about the iPhone Duo. Sure, it apes almost everything we know about modern folding phones from Samsung and Google, but with a couple of interesting twists. Keeping the under-display camera and stylus support from earlier Galaxy Z-series entries? A very smooth transition between inner and outer displays? A Made You Look clone but with Snoopy? I might prefer Android to iOS, but at the end of the day, I’m only human.

But no matter how “modern” the iPhone Duo appears at first glance compared to Google and Samsung’s respective first-gen entries, it loses out on one big metric: bulk. The iPhone Duo measures in at 11.3mm thick when closed and weighs a whopping 254 grams. Compared to Apple’s most recent foldable rivals, that’s 15 grams (or three nickels worth) heavier than the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, 39 grams heavier than the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and a whopping 53 grams heavier than the similarly-shaped Fold 8. Each of those phones is significantly thinner too, ranging anywhere between 8.9mm to 10.1mm when closed.

iPhone Duo: 254g, 11.3mm closed

Pixel 11 Pro Fold: 239g, 10.1mm closed

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra: 215g, 8.9mm closed

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: 201g, 9.7mm closed

It is, undoubtedly, a miss from Apple’s design, especially considering the push for lightweight devices with last year’s iPhone Air. However — and here’s where I have betray the most dedicated Android fans just a tiny bit — while I absolutely think Apple’s foldable is bulkier and heavier than it should be in 2026, I can’t pretend like Google is that far ahead here. Yes, this year’s foldable finally managed to shed a few grams, but the iPhone Duo still manages to be lighter than 2025’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold, a device Google was pushing to users but a month ago. Samsung, though? It’s eating Apple’s lunch all day.

	

I also have no idea how much of that extra bulk can be chalked up to Apple Pencil support. Samsung upset a pretty sizable portion of its audience when it dropped the S Pen from the Galaxy Z Fold 7, but that sacrifice came with a significantly slimmer and lighter chassis. Comparing the iPhone Duo to 2024’s Fold 6 — the last foldable Samsung shipped with stylus support — it measures in at 12.1mm thick. That said, the Fold 6 still had Apple beat on weight, even with a device that’s now over two years old.

At the end of the day, the size and weight of the iPhone Duo really only matters if you’re completely platform-agnostic, a foldable-first fan who simply wants the most refined hardware experience around. I expect most Android fans won’t be tempted with a big-screen experience not all too dissimilar from what they’ve had access to for the better part of a decade now, and I expect iOS fans who have held out for an Apple-made foldable won’t be put off by a device that’s a bit bulkier than its rivals. But hey, if you’re an early adopter looking to lord something over your Apple-loving co-workers in a couple of months, you’ve already found your first opportunity.

title: Pixel 11 gets early September update, not Android 17 QPR1 [U: OTA images]
snippet: We’re expecting the stable release of Android 17 QPR1 in September. Before that, Google is rolling out an out-of-cycle update to the Pixel 11 series with a September 2026 security patch. more…
fullText:
We’re expecting the stable release of Android 17 QPR1 in September. Before that, Google is rolling out an out-of-cycle update to the Pixel 11 series with a September 2026 security patch.

Update 9/9: Following the on-device update that some users received last week, Google has posted updated factory and OTA images for manual install. The September 1 patch ended in A1, while today’s release is B1.

It comes as not all users received last week’s OTA, with Google appearing to pull the update at some point. Those that received the previous update are getting another one that comes in at 97~ MB.  

The four updates for the Pixel 11, 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL, and 11 Pro Fold are labeled “Sep 2026.” Curiously, Google has yet to announce the Android 17 QPR1 update and expected Pixel Drop.

	

Original 9/1: On Tuesday afternoon, Pixel 11 series users received an OTA update to CD1A.260905.001.A1 (from CD1A.260714.001.A9).

The Android security update level is “September 1, 2026.” (Note: Not September 5.) The install screen has the usual generic security message: “This update fixes critical bugs and improves the performance and stability of your device.”

So far, we have reports of an under 100 MB OTA hitting the Pixel 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL, and 11 Pro Fold. Google has yet to post factory or OTA images as of Tuesday afternoon.

This is not Android 17 QPR1. Several of the visual changes coming in that release are not yet present, so this is still the initial release of Android 17.

Rather, Google is likely rolling out this update as a hot patch for Pixel 11 issues discovered since last month’s launch. The fact Google did not wait for Android 17 QPR1 should be telling.

title: Hands-on: Dbrand’s MNML Pixel 11 Pro cases are simply good, and that’s the point [Gallery]
snippet: Dbrand is definitely best-known for its flashy skins and bombastic personality, but the company is now launching a more subtle brand in “MNML,” aiming to offer dead-simple cases that are comfortable and have good quality. These are available for the latest Pixel 11 Pro phones and, in person, they certainly get the job done. more…
fullText:
Dbrand is definitely best-known for its flashy skins and bombastic personality, but the company is now launching a more subtle brand in “MNML,” aiming to offer dead-simple cases that are comfortable and have good quality. These are available for the latest Pixel 11 Pro phones and, in person, they certainly get the job done.

Available in four colors – black, navy, tan, and burgundy – MNML cases are true to their (shortened) name. The case lacks any notable branding outside of the four letters off to the side. The buttons have a metallic finish, while the case itself is a polymer material with a rough texture.

In the hand, it’s grippy without being too grippy – looking at you, Google and Samsung – while not being overly thick either. Over the past couple of years, I’ve been going caseless more and more often, but this is exactly the sort of case I would want to use, as it’s not adding a ton of unnecessary bulk. 

On Pixel 11 Pro XL, the cutouts and fit are both absolutely perfect – it helps that there’s no SIM tray to worry about, which I recently found out dbrand bafflingly leaves inaccessible in its full-coverage skins (this is dumb). The buttons are clicky, though the chunky shape and size feels a little weird to the touch. I wish the power button had a different texture so as to stand out.

	

The built-in magnets are very strong too, perhaps even more so than the array already found in Pixel 11 Pro.

These are dead simple cases, and in a way an upgraded version of the infamous Spigen Thin Fit. It feels better than the Thin Fit usually does while having 10% more personality in its colors. 

At $40 a pop (discounted if you buy multiple), it’s not cheap. But it’s a good case across the board, so you won’t regret picking one up.

title: Apple planning three major changes for its retail stores, per report
snippet: Apple is preparing “major changes” to its retail stores, according to a new report from Bloomberg. Perhaps most notably, the changes include bringing back the iconic dedicated Genius Bars. more…
fullText:
Apple is preparing “major changes” to its retail stores, according to a new report from Bloomberg. Perhaps most notably, the changes include bringing back the iconic dedicated Genius Bars.

Big Apple Store changes are coming soon

In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Mark Gurman has all the details of these changes. He says Apple plans to “accelerate” the pace at which it renovates retail stores in the coming years. As part of this, there are “three major changes” set for the renovated stores.

First, Apple plans to revamp the “Avenue” sections in its retail stores, the areas alongside Apple Stores where accessories and Apple services are promoted.

Gurman explains that Apple plans to add two new Avenue sections dedicated to online pickups and Today at Apple sessions.

Right now, many stores have a dedicated pickup table and a large seating area for the Today at Apple workshops. Those functions will move to the sides of stores within 10-foot sections known internally as bays.

The Avenue bay for online pickups will be constructed entirely from wood. The upper half will feature a subtle Apple logo, while the lower portion will contain secure drawers for storing pickup orders. A table in front will give employees a place to manage the handoff process.

The dedicated Today at Apple bay will include a large display, as well as secure drawers where instructors can store devices.

The next major change is the “removal of the giant video walls” located at the back of most stores. These video walls are used for Today at Apple sessions and marketing, but Apple plans to ditch them as part of this revamp.

The third change is a return to “dedicated Genius Bars,” Gurman says. Apple moved away from the Genius Bar design in favor of the “Genius Grove” more than a decade ago.

In many stores, Apple will replace the video walls with dedicated Genius Bars, marking a return to a familiar element from an earlier era.

The design resembles the Genius Bars of the past but with an all-wood look. There will be two counter heights for accessibility, while the wall behind the bar will include storage drawers and large posters highlighting new products.

Gurman says Apple’s goal is to realign its stores to focus on “more traditional and practical retail, service and fulfillment functions.”

title: The iPhone Duo didn’t reinvent Android foldables, but I fear the copycats anyway
snippet: Apple’s first foldable is here and, shocker, it didn’t exactly reinvent the foldable, but the iPhone Duo did get some of the most important aspects right, and will give the Android side of the conversation some things to work on too. 9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here. more…
fullText:
Apple’s first foldable is here and, shocker, it didn’t exactly reinvent the foldable, but the iPhone Duo did get some of the most important aspects right, and will give the Android side of the conversation some things to work on too.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

Look, I promise we’ll stop talking about the iPhone Duo at some point. We’re not 9to5Mac, but Apple’s first foldable is a big deal for the Android side of the industry too. It’s not every day that an entirely new form factor built up by Android brands gets co-opted by the only real competitor. 

And, despite Android’s several-year head start, Apple is immediately putting up a fierce competition with its iPhone Duo.

	

It’s a polished foldable across the board. A smart design with aspect ratios that should prove useful – and, based on the Fold 8’s popularity, resonate among customers – and a package that seems to deliver on everything it needs to. It’s thicker and heavier than basically every other current Android foldable, but it’s also not so far out of the ordinary as to be uncompetitive. Early reactions have been positive, though I’m certainly curious to see what people think after the typical Apple event psychosis wears off.

But, as good as the Duo looks, I think the biggest thing to walk away with is that Apple is not reinventing the foldable. It’s been speculated for years now that Apple would somehow crack open the formula on how to build a foldable in ways that no Android brand had figured out and, based on what’s been shown off so far, that’s simply not the case.

On the hardware side, Apple doesn’t seem to outdo existing hardware in any particularly meaningful ways. The matte display is the thing that has my attention most, as it seems to lessen even the visual appearance of a crease to essentially nothing – though, without that, I bet it’d be similar to the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Oppo Find N6. But even that display doesn’t seem flawless, with the glossy dot over the selfie camera immediately catching my attention. Under-display cameras are already a tech that’s been shown to be of dubious worth, and with this visual oddity at play, I’m pretty surprised Apple adopted this one at all.

via Brian Tong
via Brian Tong
iPhone Duo hands-on videos reveal Android foldable pain points we know too well

The software is where even I expected Apple to figure out ideas for a foldable beyond what we’ve seen but, really, there wasn’t much.

Split-screen looks mostly akin to the Pixel Fold, though with the two halves treated as independent by default and allowing you to go to the homescreen to grab another app. That feels very intuitive, even if Android has the same core functionality through its taskbar. The ability to put video windows on top of other apps looks useful and more polished than existing split-screen or picture-in-picture options on Android, but it’s still not exactly groundbreaking. 

The most attention-grabbing additions in Apple’s software come from a neat animation that shows up when you open or close the device – almost certainly set to be copied in future software updates on Android devices – and a rethinking of navigation.

Apple is moving app controls and the status bar to the side of the UI rather than the top and bottom where they’re resided for ages now. It gives me mixed feelings. The utility of offloading those controls to the side of the display to make vertical content feel more at home on the wider aspect ratio makes sense, but it also looks wildly ugly to me, or unbalanced at the very least.

All of this is to say, Apple didn’t break any new ground here, and they still have to deal with many of the same problems.

Like every existing foldable, Apple has some different ideas to add into the core experience, but that core experience is essentially the same – it’s just based on iOS this time. Android “got it right” in terms of that core experience, and now everyone has a chance to sit down and think about where to take it next. In a way, it reminds me of the whole app drawer situation. Android got this right years ago, and Apple brought in its own version that’s the same core idea, just different (and much worse, but I digress).

What worries me is the idea that Android manufacturers are going to rush to copy what Apple has put out. 

There’s nothing on the iPhone Duo, at least not yet, that feels worth copying – except maybe that aforementioned animation. The sidebar setup, for instance, acknowledges a problem that these new form factors are facing. Modern smartphones are all tall and narrow slabs, so wide designs aren’t a thought for developers. By offloading everything to the side, Apple is presenting a solution for the lack of space for content that devices like Fold 8 have to give up for the sake of top and bottom bars. I’m just personally not sure it’s the right solution. As just one example, this UI decision sounds awful for anyone who uses their phone in their left hand (which, hello, that’s me). At least the top and bottom bars are equally a little bit uncomfortable for everyone.

It’s a bold new chapter in the foldable market, and Apple is surely set to sell a lot of these. I’m perhaps most surprised that it’s competitively priced – cheaper than Samsung’s top foldable, too! On top of that, I think the Duo will be a net-positive for Android foldables in the long run. The creativity of iOS developers could bring some new ideas to Android in time as new eyes look at these form factors, and it’s also going to force accessory makers to finally take foldables seriously.

What do you think of the iPhone Duo and how it relates to Android foldables?

title: Apple ranks third on TIME’s World’s Best Companies list after last year’s absence
snippet: TIME’s “The World’s Best Companies 2026” list is out, with Apple returning at No. 3 after dropping off the ranking last year. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
TIME’s “The World’s Best Companies 2026” list is out, with Apple returning at No. 3 after dropping off the ranking last year. Here are the details.

Apple returns to TIME’s World’s Best Companies list

Apple’s performance on TIME’s The World’s Best Companies list has been rather interesting.

After topping the list in 2024, the company was notably absent from last year’s list “due to a decline in revenue from 2022 to 2024, which many Wall Street analysts have postulated could be due to the company falling behind on AI,” said TIME.

At the time (no pun intended), the publication also noted:

“But tides may be turning as the behemoth figures out its footing in the new tech landscape; CEO Tim Cook said on a third quarter earnings call that the company is significantly growing investments in AI, embedding it across devices and platforms. In July, after the study period for this list, Apple reported a 10% year-over-year revenue growth—the biggest bump since 2021.”

This week, TIME published its 2026 list, which saw Apple return to third place with a 93.16 overall score, behind Cigna at 94.37 and Nvidia, which topped the list at 97.51.

TIME calculates the score based on three equally weighted factors: employee satisfaction, revenue growth over the previous three years, and sustainability transparency. The three scores are combined into an overall rating out of 100.

Apple also ranked third for employee satisfaction, behind Microsoft and IBM, which ranked first and second, respectively. In sustainability transparency, however, Apple fell to 24th after topping that category in 2024.

TIME also gave Apple a “Very High” rating for revenue growth, the highest of its four designations, ahead of “Outstanding,” “High,” and “Moderate.”

Here’s the top 10 of TIME’s 2026 World’s Best Companies ranking:

title: Counterpoint: Apple foldable panel shipments could rise 167% by 2030
snippet: Counterpoint Research has released a new report examining the impact of the iPhone Duo on the foldable smartphone market, display suppliers, and the segment’s growth through 2030. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Counterpoint Research has released a new report examining the impact of the iPhone Duo on the foldable smartphone market, display suppliers, and the segment’s growth through 2030. Here are the details.

Apple to account for 27% of 2026 foldable panel shipments

In a new report published yesterday, Counterpoint Research outlines broadly similar expectations to those set by TrendForce for the iPhone Duo’s performance through the end of 2026.

According to Counterpoint, Apple is expected to account for 27% of foldable smartphone panel shipments in 2026, despite the iPhone Duo launching only next month.

Samsung, meanwhile, is expected to retain the top spot with a 33% share, following an 8% year-over-year increase in shipments. Huawei is forecast to rank third with a 25% share, two percentage points behind Apple, as its shipments decline 6%.

Looking further ahead, Counterpoint expects foldable panel shipments to grow 74% between 2026 and 2030, “equivalent to a compound annual growth rate of about 15%.”

The report notes that “Apple shipments are forecast to increase 167% from their H2-only 2026 base to 2030, lifting the brand’s share by about 15 percentage points to 42%,” while Samsung’s shipments are expected to grow 27%, even as its share falls to 24%. Huawei, in turn, is forecast to see shipments rise just 3%, with its share declining to 15%.

Finally, Counterpoint also forecasts how foldable panel shipments will break down across in-fold, multi-fold, and clamshell designs by 2030:

In-fold panel shipments are forecast to grow 79% from 2026 to 2030, raising their share from 81% to 84%. Multi-fold shipments are expected to increase 179%, lifting their share from 2.8% to 4.5%. Clamshell shipments are forecast to grow 27%, but their share would decline by about 4 percentage points to 12%.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 makes a big change to a small complication that I’m excited about
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 is a major upgrade to the core health and fitness tracking wearable. That’s because of the new Health Sensing System that includes an even more capable heart rate monitor. The new hardware doesn’t just extend to more accurate health data. There’s a big change to a small complication that I’m seeing in Apple’s marketing material. It’s just one thing I’m excited about with the new Series 12 and Ultra 4 models. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 is a major upgrade to the core health and fitness tracking wearable. That’s because of the new Health Sensing System that includes an even more capable heart rate monitor. 

The new hardware doesn’t just extend to more accurate health data. There’s a big change to a small complication that I’m seeing in Apple’s marketing material. It’s just one thing I’m excited about with the new Series 12 and Ultra 4 models.

Apple’s Heart Rate complication gets an upgrade on Series 12 and Ultra 4 models

I really like glancing at my Apple Watch and seeing my recent heart rate. Keeping my resting heart rate low is a good indicator that I’m doing something right with fitness (and managing stress).

For that reason, I often use Apple’s Heart Rate complication on my watch face. 

The small, circular version is just a launcher that displays the Heart Rate app icon. The wide version, though, displays a recent heart rate reading, plus a graph of your heart rate since midnight. 

I use the wide version since it actually displays information. The app launcher version doesn’t have much utility for me.

Based on Apple’s Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 marketing material, however, it looks like the smaller heart rate complication is getting a big upgrade.

Apple shows it displaying an actual heart rate for the first time. That means it can be one of the smaller complication sides, not just a three-wide version. 

The same complication is still just an app launcher on watchOS 27’s release candidate version on Apple Watch Series 11 and Ultra 3.

The reason is probably because the new Health Sensing System reads heart rate every five seconds, a 60x increase over previous Apple Watch versions.

This means the complication can display a live result. The wide version needs space to provide context for when the heart reading was recorded. 

This kind of small change is the sort of thing that adds up and makes for an overall better product that all users can appreciate. 

Apple Watch Series 12 is currently available for pre-order from $399. Apple Watch Ultra 4 is available for pre-order from $799. Both models launch in one week on September 18.

title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs Ultra 3: Here’s everything new
snippet: Apple Watch Ultra 4 has the same external look as Ultra 3, but it’s packed with internal upgrades to the chip and health sensors that unlock new and improved features. Here’s everything new in Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs Ultra 3. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Ultra 4 has the same external look as Ultra 3, but it’s packed with internal upgrades to the chip and health sensors that unlock new and improved features. Here’s everything new in Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs Ultra 3.

Performance: S11 chip and 4GB RAM

Apple often includes a new chip with its latest Watch models, but most chip updates include only minor changes and minimal performance gains. And last year, Apple opted to stick with the same S10 from 2024.

But Apple Watch Ultra 4 has a brand-new S11 chip. S11 unlocks exclusive new software features thanks to its more powerful capabilities.

Apple doesn’t give specific benchmarks to measure the improvements, only saying S11 is its “most powerful wearable chip.”

Apple Watch Ultra 4 also doubles the memory of Ultra 3, with 4GB versus the 2GB of last year’s model.

Health: All-new, more powerful sensors

Apple Watch Ultra 4 has an all-new Health Sensing System that might be the biggest change ever to the Watch’s internal sensors. Apple says the new system “unlocks deeper health and fitness insights.”

Here’s the breakdown of feature improvements, per Apple:

Heart rate tracking: Second-generation electrical heart sensor and always-on optical heart sensor enable high-frequency background heart rate tracking that you can view on new heart rate watch face complication

HRV improvements: “now measured up to 24 times more often and available to view in a new section of the Heart Rate app”

New Recovery HRV: “best for identifying daily signals of stress and recovery”

Step tracking: More accurate, with new Steps complication to track steps in real time from watch face

Battery: Lasts longer and charges faster

One of Apple Watch Ultra’s best features is battery life, and Ultra 4 delivers noteworthy gains in that department. Here’s the comparison:

Apple Watch Ultra 4: up to 50 hours battery life, or 84 hours in Low Power Mode

Apple Watch Ultra 3: up to 42 hours battery life, or 72 hours in Low Power Mode

Apple Watch Ultra 4 can also provide 50% more battery life on a quick 15-minute charge. 15 minutes gets you 18 hours of runtime, versus only 12 on Apple Watch Ultra 3.

Exclusive software features: Readiness app and Audio Intelligence

Readiness is a health feature that’s become common with other wearables, and now Apple has its own version with a Readiness app. Here’s what it does per Apple:

Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduces readiness, a new feature that analyzes a user’s recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score to offer insight into their capacity for the day ahead. Readiness provides a single 0-10 score each day with a clear, actionable recommendation: Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It. This helps a user decide how to take on their day, whether they’re headed into a workday or tackling their training plan.

As mentioned above, Ultra 4 also adds new watch face complications for tracking your steps and heart rate.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 will additionally support a suite of Audio Intelligence features, some of which are coming in a software update later this year. Audio Intelligence includes:

Sound Recognition: “[alerts] users who are deaf or hard of hearing of important sounds, even when their iPhone isn’t with them. This feature listens for sounds like sirens, alarms, doorbells, or a baby crying, and uses on-device intelligence to notify users when they’re detected.”

Live Rewind: “[helps] users recall what was just said in conversation. A double press of the Digital Crown shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, so users can catch something they may have missed or are less familiar with.”

Siri Recap: [creates] high-level summaries of conversations that users can review later to jog their memory. When Siri Recap is turned on, after a conversation, Apple Intelligence automatically generates a title and key points in the new Siri app, allowing users to be more present and engaged in the moment.”

Shazam: “instantly detects the music playing around the user and automatically displays the song title and artist’s name on the Music Recognition widget in the Smart Stack”

title: Apple shares the data behind Apple Watch Series 12’s biggest health claim
snippet: Apple makes a bold claim when it comes to Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. According to Apple, the new Health Sensing System on both watches “delivers the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” Apple backs up this claim with a new study that shows how Series 12 heart rate sensing compares to other leading wearables, including smart rings and fitness bands. more…
fullText:
Apple makes a bold claim when it comes to Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. According to Apple, the new Health Sensing System on both watches “delivers the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” Apple backs up this claim with a new study that shows how Series 12 heart rate sensing compares to other leading wearables, including smart rings and fitness bands.

Health Sensing System is a major upgrade for Apple Watch

Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are a major upgrade due to the Health Sensing System that drives many of the health and fitness features.

“With the release of Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, Apple introduced the Health Sensing System, which includes both updated electrical and optical (photoplethysmography, or PPG) heart sensors and associated signal processing algorithms, as well as several features enabled by the new technology, such as Recovery HRV and the Readiness app,” Apple explains.

How Apple tested Series 12

According to Apple’s nine-page study, testing took place across five sites in the US and Malaysia during July and August 2026. Apple enrolled 1,460 adults, with 1,254 contributing at least one paired measurement to the final analysis.

Participants wore Apple Watch Series 12 on one wrist and a competing wrist-based device on the other. A Polar H10 ECG chest strap served as the reference.

Apple compared Series 12 against the Garmin Forerunner 970, Google Pixel Watch 4, Huawei Watch 5, Samsung Galaxy Watch 8, and WHOOP 5. Participants also wore an Oura Ring 5 on an index finger, following Oura’s guidance.

The tests covered outdoor running, treadmill intervals, cycling, high-intensity interval training, and strength training. Apple also measured background heart rate during everyday activities including resting, desk work, meal preparation, and walking.

These scenarios included challenges such as rapid wrist movement, changing heart rates, and the “cadence lock” that can cause an optical sensor to mistake running rhythm for a pulse.

What Apple found

Apple says Series 12 produced statistically better overall accuracy than every comparison device across both workouts and daily living. Across 159 individual activity and measurement comparisons, Apple Watch achieved statistically better accuracy in 139.

You can read the study and see the results in full here.

Apple Watch Series 12 is currently available for pre-order from $399. Apple Watch Ultra 4 is available for pre-order from $799. Both models launch in one week on September 18.
